Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 10, verse 1:

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Tafsir of Surat Yunus (peace be upon him). Surat Yunus is Meccan according to al-Hasan, Ikrimah, 'Ata' and Jabir. Ibn 'Abbas said: except for three verses, from His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿If you are in doubt﴾ [Yunus: 94] to the end of them. Muqatil said: except for two verses, namely His saying, "If you are in doubt," which were revealed in Medina. Al-Kalbi said: it is Meccan except for His saying: ﴿And among them are those who believe in it and among them are those who do not believe in it﴾ [Yunus: 40], which was revealed in Medina concerning the Jews. A group said: about forty verses from its beginning were revealed in Mecca and the rest in Medina.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

Alif, Lam, Ra. These are the verses of the Wise Book.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Alif, Lam, Ra﴾. An-Nahhas said: It was recited to Abu Ja'far Ahmad ibn Shu'ayb ibn 'Ali ibn al-Husayn ibn Hurayth, who said: 'Ali ibn al-Husayn informed us, from his father, from Yazid, that Ikrimah narrated to him from Ibn 'Abbas: "Alif, Lam, Ra", "Ha, Mim", and "Nun" are the letters of "al-Rahman" separated. I related this to al-A'mash, and he said: "Do you have similar things and do not tell me about them?" And from Ibn 'Abbas also, he said: the meaning of "Ra" is: "I am Allah, I see." An-Nahhas said: I saw Abu Ishaq inclining to this view, because Sibawayh has related something similar from the Arabs and recited:

"With good, good things, though they be evil..." And I do not desire evil [Footnote: I will repay you with good; and if it comes from you as evil, it will be from me in like manner, and I do not desire evil except that you wish it.] (from Sharh al-Shawahid), except that ta...

Al-Hasan and Ikrimah said: "Ra" is an oath. Sa'id, from Qatadah, said: "Ra" is the name of the surah; he said: and likewise every spelled-out letter sequence in the Qur'an. Mujahid said: they are the openings of the surahs. Muhammad ibn Yazid said: they are an alert (tanbih), and likewise the letters of spelling (huruf al-tahajji). It is recited as "Ra" without imalah, and it is recited with imalah lest it resemble "ma" and "la" among the letters.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿These are the verses of the Wise Book﴾ is an inchoative and a predicate, meaning: these which have been mentioned are the verses of the Wise Book. Mujahid and Qatadah said: He intended the Torah, the Gospel and the earlier books, for "tilka" is a demonstrative for a feminine absent referent. It was also said: "tilka" carries the sense of "hadhihi" (this), meaning: these are the verses of the Wise Book. From this is the saying of al-A'sha:

"Those are my horses from it, and those are my mounts; their young are yellow like raisins..."

That is, "these are my horses." What is meant is the Qur'an, and this is more correct, because no mention of the earlier books has preceded, and because "al-Hakim" is an attribute of the Qur'an. Its evidence is His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Alif, Lam, Ra. A Book whose verses have been perfected﴾ [Hud: 1]. This meaning has been discussed earlier at the beginning of Surat al-Baqarah. Al-Hakim means: that which is made firm (muhkam) with the lawful and the unlawful, the limits and the rulings; so said Abu 'Ubaydah and others. It was also said: al-Hakim carries the sense of al-Hakim (the judge), meaning that He is judge concerning the lawful and the unlawful, and judge among people with truth; so it is fa'il in the sense of fa'il. Its evidence is His saying: ﴿And He sent down with them the Book in truth, that it might judge between the people concerning that over which they differed﴾ [al-Baqarah: 213]. It was also said: al-Hakim carries the sense of the one judged (al-mahkum fihi), meaning that Allah has judged in it with justice and benevolence and giving to the kinsfolk, and has judged in it with the prohibition of indecency and wrongdoing, and with Paradise for whoever obeys Him and the Fire for whoever disobeys Him; so it is fa'il in the sense of maf'ul; so said al-Hasan and others. Muqatil said: al-Hakim carries the sense of the one made firm (al-muhkam) against falsehood, in which there is no lie and no contradiction; so it is fa'il in the sense of maf'al, like the saying of al-A'sha describing his qasidah which he composed:

"And a strange poem that comes to kings, wise, which I composed so that it might be said: who composed it?"

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 10, verse 2:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Is it a wonder for the people?﴾ This is an interrogative (istifham) whose meaning is affirmation (taqrir) and rebuke (tawbikh). "ʿAjaban" is the predicate (khabar) of kana, and its subject (ism) is "an awhayna" (that We revealed), which is in the place of nominative case (raf'), meaning: Our revelation was a wonder to the people. In the reading of ʿAbd Allah, it is "ʿajabun," with the subject of kana being "ʿajabun," and the predicate being "an awhayna."

(to a man from among them) It is read "rajlin" with the letter jim pronounced with sukun. The occasion of revelation (sabab al-nuzul), as related from Ibn ʿAbbas, is that when Muhammad was sent, the disbelievers said: "God is greater than that His messenger should be a human being." And they said: "God found no one to send but the orphan of Abu Talib." So it was revealed: "Is it a wonder for the people," meaning the people of Makkah, "a wonder?" It is also said that they only marveled at the mention of resurrection (al-baʿth).

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿that warn the people and give good news to those who believe﴾ is in the place of the accusative (nasb) by the removal of the preposition, meaning: "that warn the people," and likewise "that for them is a sure footing of truth (qadam sidq)." The meanings of warning (indharah) and good news (bishharah), and other words of this verse, have already been discussed [see vol. 1 pp. 184 and 238]. The meaning of "qadam sidq" has been disputed. Ibn ʿAbbas said: qadam sidq is a station of truth (manzil sidq), its evidence being His saying: ﴿And say: My Lord, cause me to enter an entrance of truth﴾ [al-Isra' 17:80] [see vol. 10 p. 312]. Also from him: a good reward for what they had sent forward of their deeds. Also from him: "qadam sidq" is the precedence of happiness in the primordial decree (al-dhikr al-awwal), and this was said by Mujahid. Al-Zajjaj said: a lofty rank. Dhu al-Rummah said:

For you is a foot that people do not deny, / along with lofty lineage, it has overflowed the sea.

Qatadah said: a previous salaf of truth. al-Rabiʿ said: a reward of truth. ʿAta' said: a station of truth. Yamani said: a faith of truth. It was also said: the supplication of the angels. It was also said: a righteous child whom they sent forward. al-Mawardi said: that the truthfulness of obedience be matched by the truthfulness of recompense. Al-Hasan and Qatadah also said: it is Muhammad ﷺ, for he is an obeyed intercessor who goes before them, as he said: (I am your forerunner (faraṭ) at the Basin) [i.e., one who goes ahead of you to it]. He ﷺ was asked about it and said: (It is my intercession; you seek a means through me to your Lord). al-Tirmidhi al-Hakim said: He ﷺ put them forward at the Praised Station (al-maqam al-mahmud). Also from al-Hasan: their calamity in the Prophet ﷺ. ʿAbd al-ʿAziz ibn Yahya said: "qadam sidq" is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, those for whom the best from Us has preceded, they will be kept far from it﴾ [al-Anbiya' 21:101] [see vol. 11 p. 345]. Muqatil said: deeds they had sent forward, and al-Tabari chose this. Al-Wadah said:

Pray to the Lord of the Throne and take a foot / that will save you on the day of stumbling and slipping.

It was also said: it is God's putting this nation forward in the gathering from the graves and in entering Paradise, as he ﷺ said: (We are the last but the first on the Day of Resurrection, the ones for whom judgment is given before all creation). Its reality is that it is a metaphor (kinayah) for striving in righteous deeds; so it was expressed by "foot," just as beneficence is expressed by "hand" and praise by "tongue." Hassan recited:

For us is the highest foot toward You, and behind us / our first ones follow in obedience to God.

He means precedence through sincere obedience, and God knows best. Abu ʿUbaydah and al-Kisa'i said: every precedence, whether of good or evil, is among the Arabs a "qadam" (foot); it is said: "So-and-so has a foot in Islam," "He has for me a qadam sidq," "a qadam sharr," "a qadam khayr." It is feminine, though it may be masculine; it is said: "qadam hasan" and "qadam salihah." Ibn al-Aʿrabi said: al-qadam is precedence in nobility. Al-ʿAjjaj said:

The sons of al-ʿAwwam slipped from the family of al-Hakam, / and left the kingship to a king of precedence.

In the Sahihayn, from the Prophet ﷺ, that he said: (I have five names: I am Muhammad, and Ahmad, and I am al-Mahi, through whom God erases disbelief; and I am al-Hashir, at whose feet (ʿala qadamī) people will be gathered; and I am al-ʿAqib). He means the last of the prophets, as the Most High said: ﴿and the Seal of the Prophets﴾ [al-Ahzab 33:40].

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿The disbelievers said: Indeed, this is clearly a sorcerer﴾. Ibn Muhaysin, Ibn Kathir, and the Kufans ʿAsim, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Khalaf, and al-Aʿmash read "lasahirun" (a sorcerer) as an attribute (naʿt) of the Messenger of God ﷺ. The rest read "lasihrun" (sorcery) as an attribute of the Qur'an. The meaning of sorcery (sihr) has already been discussed in "al-Baqarah" [see vol. 2 p. 43].

**Its saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, your Lord is Allah, who created the heavens and the earth in six days and then established Himself above the Throne﴾** [[See vol. 7, p. 218.]].

**(He arranges the affair)**. Mujahid said: He decrees it and determines it alone. Ibn 'Abbas said: No one shares with Him in the management of His creation. It was said: He sends down the command. It was said: He descends with it. It was said: He orders it and carries it out. The meanings are close to one another. Jibril is for revelation, Mika'il for rain, Israfil for the Trumpet, and 'Izra'il for taking souls. Its real meaning is the placing of affairs in their proper ranks according to the rulings of their outcomes, and it is derived from *al-dubr* (the back, i.e., what comes after). *Al-amr* (the affair) is a collective noun for affairs.

**(There is no intercessor)** is in the place of a nominative, and the meaning is "there is no intercessor" **(except after His permission)**. The meaning of intercession (*shafa'ah*) has already been discussed in "al-Baqarah" [[See vol. 3, p. 273.]]. No one, whether a prophet or other than a prophet, intercedes except by the permission of Him, glorified is He. This is a refutation of the unbelievers' saying about those they worshipped besides Allah: ﴿These are our intercessors with Allah﴾ [[See p. 321 of this part.]] [Yunus: 18]. So Allah informed them that no one intercedes for anyone except with His permission, so how much less the intercession of idols that do not understand.

**Its saying, exalted is He: ﴿That is Allah, your Lord, so worship Him﴾**. That is, the One who did these things, such as creating the heavens and the earth, is your Lord, and there is no lord for you other than Him. **"So worship Him"**, that is, make Him one and devote worship sincerely to Him.

**(Will you not remember?)**, that is, that these are His creatures, so that you may reason from them to Him.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 10, verse 4:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿To Him is your return, all of you﴾. It (ilayhi, "to Him") is in the nominative case, as the subject of a nominal sentence (marfu' bil-ibtida'). "Jami'an" (all of you) is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (manṣub 'ala al-hal). The meaning of "return to Allah" is the return to His parts (ajza'ihi).

﴿The promise of Allah, in truth﴾: both words are verbal nouns (masdarani), meaning that Allah promised that promise and fulfilled it. "Haqqan" (in truth) means truthfulness with no failing in it. Ibrahim ibn Abi 'Abla read "wa'da Allahi haqqun" (the promise of Allah is true) as a new independent sentence (al-isti'naf).

His saying, the Exalted: "Innahu yabda'u al-khalq" (Indeed He originates creation), that is, from dust. "Thumma yu'iduhu" (then He repeats it) to it. Mujahid said: He brings it into being, then causes it to die, then gives it life for the Resurrection; or He brings it into being from water, then repeats it from state to state. Yazid ibn al-Qa'qa' read "innahu yabda'u al-khalq," where "anna" (that) is in the accusative position, meaning: He promised you that He originates creation. It is also permissible that the implied sense is "because He originates creation," as one says: "Labbayka, inna al-hamda wa al-ni'mata laka" (I answer You, indeed the praise and the blessing are Yours), and the kasra (inna with a short i) is better. Al-Farra' permitted that "anna" be in the nominative position, so that it functions as a subject. Ahmad ibn Yahya said: the implied sense is "truly, its originating of creation."

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿That He may recompense those who believed and did righteous deeds with justice﴾, that is, with justice.

﴿And those who disbelieved, for them is a drink of scalding water﴾: that is, water that is hot and whose heat has reached its extreme; "hamimah" is similar to it. It is said: "hamamtu al-ma' ahummuhu, fahuwa hamim," meaning "mahmum" (heated), with fa'il in the sense of maf'ul. And everything heated among the Arabs is "hamim."

﴿And a painful punishment﴾: that is, causing pain, whose agony reaches their hearts.

﴿Because they used to disbelieve﴾: that is, because of their disbelief. Most of the Quraysh acknowledged that Allah is their Creator, so He argued against them with this, saying: Whoever is able to originate is able to repeat after annihilation or after the dispersal of the parts.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 10, verse 5:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿It is He who made the sun a radiance﴾. It has two objects, meaning "shining" (mudi'a). It is not feminized because it is a maṣdar (verbal noun), or it means "possessing radiance" (dhāt ḍiyā'). ﴿And the moon a light﴾ is coordinated with it, meaning "giving light" (munīran), or "possessing light" (dhā nūr). Ḍiyā' is that which illuminates things, while nūr is that which makes things clear but is then hidden, because both come from fire, from a single origin. Ḍiyā' is the plural of ḍaw', like sayyāṭ and ḥiyāḍ are the plurals of sawṭ and ḥawḍ.

Qunbul, on the authority of Ibn Kathir, read "ḍi'ā'an" with a hamza on the yā', and there is no basis for this, because its yā' was originally a fatḥah-marked wāw, and it is the ʿayn of the verb; its original form is ḍiwā'an, which was changed into yā', as it was changed in al-ṣiyām and al-qiyām. Al-Mahdawi said: whoever reads ḍi'ā' with the hamza, it is metathesized (maqlūb): the hamza that comes after the alif was moved so that it came before the alif, becoming ḍi'āyan, then the yā' was changed into a hamza because it occurred after an extra alif. Likewise, if you assume that the yā', when it was placed later, reverted to the wāw from which it had changed, it is also changed into a hamza, so its pattern is fi'āl, metathesized from fi'āl... (as stated). It is said that the sun and the moon illuminate their faces for the people of the seven heavens, and their appearance is for the people of the seven earths.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and determined for it stations﴾, meaning "possessing stations" (dhā manāzil), or "He determined for it stations." Then it is said: the meaning is "and He determined them (both)," so the singular is used for brevity and concision, as He said: "And when they see a trade or a diversion, they break away toward it" [see vol. 18, p. 901]. And as the poet said:

We are with what we have, and you are with what you have, content, though our opinions differ.

It is also said that the report is about the moon alone, since by it the months are counted, upon which dealings and the like depend, as was mentioned in al-Baqarah [see vol. 2, p. 341 and following]. And in Surah Ya Sin: ﴿And the moon, We have determined for it stations﴾ [see vol. 15, p. 29] [Ya Sin: 39], meaning according to the number of the month, which is twenty-eight stations, and two days for the waning and the disappearance [al-maḥāq (with three vowel forms): the end of the month when it has disappeared and is not seen], and its explanation will come there.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿so that you may know the number of years and the reckoning﴾. Ibn ʿAbbas said: if He had made two suns, one sun by day and one sun by night, with no darkness or night in them, the number of years and the reckoning of months would not be known. The singular of "al-sinin" is sanah, and among the Arabs some say sanawāt in the plural, and some say sanahāt. Its diminutive is sunayyah and sunayhah.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿God did not create that except with truth﴾, meaning that Allah, Mighty and Majestic, did not intend by creating that anything but wisdom and rightness, and to manifest His craftsmanship and wisdom, and as a sign of His power and knowledge, and so that every soul may be recompensed for what it has earned. This is the truth.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿He details the signs for a people who know﴾. Detailing the signs is making them clear so that they may be taken as evidence of His power, Exalted is He, through the specialization of the night with its darkness and the day with its light, without any entitlement to them or obligation; so this is for them an evidence that this is by the will of one who wills. Ibn Kathir, Abu ʿAmr, Hafs and Yaʿqub read "yufassilu" with the yā', and Abu ʿUbayd and Abu Hatim preferred it, because of His saying before it: "God did not create that except with truth," and after it: "and what God created in the heavens and the earth," so that it follows it. Ibn al-Sumayqaʿ read "tufaṣṣalu" with a ḍammah on the tā' and a fatḥah on the ṣād, as a passive verb, with "al-āyāt" in the nominative. The rest read "nufaṣṣilu" with the nūn, as a plural of majesty.

Its meaning has already been discussed in al-Baqarah and elsewhere [see vol. 2, p. 191], and praise be to God. It has been said that the occasion of its revelation was that the people of Makkah asked for a sign, and God directed them to reflect on His creations and consider them. This is related from Ibn 'Abbas. "For a people who are mindful" means mindful of shirk (associating partners with God). As for one who associates partners with God and does not reason from the signs, the verse is not a sign for him.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 10, verse 7–8:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, those who do not expect to meet Us﴾ — "yarjuna" means "yakhafuna" (fear), and from it is the saying of the poet:

When a bee has stung him, he does not expect (yarju) its sting, and he avoids it, (going) to the honey of a hive that is full of bees ... and [[The verse is by Abu Dhu'ayb. His saying "wa-kHalifuha" with the dotted kha: he came to its honey while it was absent, grazing. It is also narrated as "wa-Halifuha" with the undotted ha, meaning he kept to it constantly. "Al-nawb" means bees, because they graze and then return (tanubu) to their place. It is also narrated as "'awamil" instead of "'awasil," and these are the ones that make honey and wax.

(From the commentary on the Diwan of Abu Dhu'ayb.)]]

It is also said that "yarjuna" means "yatma'una" (hope), and from it is the saying of another:

Do the sons of Marwan expect (yarju) my hearing and obedience, while my people, Tamim, and the deserts are behind me?

So al-rajaʾ (expectation) may carry the meaning of fear and of hope, i.e., they do not fear punishment and do not hope for reward. The meeting with punishment and reward has been made a meeting with God, as a magnification of both. It is also said: the meeting is taken in its apparent sense, which is sight, i.e., they do not hope to see Us. Some scholars said: rajaʾ in the sense of fear occurs only with denial, as in His saying, the Exalted: ﴿What is the matter with you that you do not expect dignity from God?﴾ [Nuh: 13]. Others said: rather, it occurs with its meaning in every context where the meaning indicates it.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And they are content with the life of this world﴾ — i.e., they were content with it in place of the Hereafter, so they worked for it.

(﴿And they are at rest in it﴾) — i.e., they rejoiced in it and settled down in it. The root of "iṭma'anna" is "ṭa'mana, ṭuma'nīnatin," so its mim was moved forward, and a nun and an alif of connection were added. Al-Ghaznawi mentioned this.

(﴿And those who are heedless of Our signs﴾) — i.e., of Our proofs — (﴿heedless﴾): they do not take heed and do not reflect.

(﴿Those, their refuge is﴾) — i.e., their dwelling and their abode.

(﴿the Fire, because of what they used to earn﴾) — i.e., because of disbelief and denial.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 10, verse 9:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, those who believe﴾, i.e., who affirm the truth.

(And do righteous deeds—their Lord guides them by their faith) i.e., He increases them in guidance [[In manuscript B: "He provides for them."]], like His saying: ﴿And those who are guided, He increases them in guidance﴾ [[See vol. 16, p. 238.]] [Muhammad: 17]. It has also been said: "Their Lord guides them by their faith" to a place beneath which rivers flow. Abu Rawq said: Their Lord guides them by their faith to Paradise. 'Atiyyah said: "He guides them" means He rewards them and recompenses them. Mujahid said: "Their Lord guides them" with light on the Path to Paradise; He makes for them a light by which they walk. And there is a report from the Prophet ﷺ that strengthens this, that he said: (The believer encounters his deed in its most beautiful form, so it comforts him and guides him; and the disbeliever encounters his deed in its most hideous form, so it frightens him and misguides him.) This is the meaning of the hadith. Ibn Jurayj said: He makes their deeds a guide for them. Al-Hasan said: "He guides them" means He shows them mercy.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Rivers flow beneath them﴾. It has been said: in the speech there is an elided waw, i.e., "and rivers flow beneath them," that is, beneath their gardens. It has also been said: beneath their couches, and this is better in terms of leisure and delight.

**Qur'anic commentary: al-Qurtubi, *al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran*, on Surah Yunus (10), verse 10**

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Their call therein is: "Glory be to You, O Allah"﴾. *Da'wahum* means their supplication (*id'a'uhum*). *Al-da'wa* is the verbal noun of *da'a, yad'u*, just as *al-shakwa* is the verbal noun of *shaka, yashku*. That is, their supplications in Paradise are that they say, "Glory be to You, O Allah." It was also said: when they wish to ask for something, they express the request in the form of glorification (*tasbih*), and they conclude with praise (*hamd*). It was also said: their calling of the servants so that they bring whatever they desire, and then they glorify God. It was also said: the word *du'a'* here means wishing (*tamanni*). Allah Exalted says: ﴿And therein you shall have whatever you wish (*ma tadda'una*)﴾ [Fussilat: 31], that is, whatever you wish for (see vol. 15, p. 43). And Allah knows best.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And their greeting therein is: "Peace"﴾. That is, their greeting from Allah, or the greeting of the angels, or the greeting of some of them to others, is "Peace." The meaning of *tahiyya* (greeting) has already been discussed fully in *al-Nisa'* (see vol. 5, p. 297). And all praise is due to Allah.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿And the last of their call is: "All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds"﴾. On this verse there are four issues.

**The first issue:** It has been said that when the people of Paradise pass by a bird and desire it, they say, "Glory be to You, O Allah." Then the angel brings them what they desire. When they have eaten, they praise Allah. Thus their request is expressed in the words of glorification, and they conclude with the words of praise.

Abu 'Ubayd did not report anything except the lightening of *anna* (i.e., *an*) with the nominative case after it. He said: "We see that they chose this and differentiated it from the saying of the Mighty and Majestic, *anna la'nata Allah* and *anna ghadaba Allah*, because they intended to report the words that are said, 'All praise is due to Allah.'"

Al-Nahhas said: the position of al-Khalil and Sibawayh is that this *an* is the lightened form of the heavy *anna*, and the meaning is that it is "All praise is due to Allah." Muhammad ibn Yazid (al-Mubarrad) said: it is permissible to say *an al-hamdu lillah*, making it operate in its light form as it operates in its heavy form, but the nominative (*raf'*) is more analogical (*aqyas*).

Al-Nahhas said: Abu Hatim reported that Bilal ibn Abi Burda recited, "*Wa akhiru da'wahum an al-hamdu lillahi rabbi al-'alamin*." I say: this is also the reading of Ibn Muhaysin, which al-Ghaznawi reported, since he transmits it from him.

**The second issue:** Glorification (*tasbih*), praise (*hamd*), and declaration of God's oneness (*tahlil*) may be called supplication (*du'a'*). Muslim and al-Bukhari reported from Ibn 'Abbas that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) used to say at times of distress: "There is no god but Allah, the Mighty, the Forbearing. There is no god but Allah, Lord of the Mighty Throne. There is no god but Allah, Lord of the heavens, Lord of the earth, and Lord of the Noble Throne."

Al-Tabari said: the early generation (*al-salaf*) would supplicate with this supplication and call it "the supplication of distress."

Ibn 'Uyayna, when asked about this, said: "Do you not know that Allah Exalted says: 'When My servant is occupied with praising Me instead of asking Me, I give him the best of what I give to those who ask'?"

What settles the dispute, and that this is called supplication even though it contains no meaning of supplication, but is merely the exaltation of Allah Exalted and praise of Him, is what al-Nasa'i reported from Sa'd ibn Abi Waqqas, who said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "The supplication of Dhu al-Nun when he supplicated with it in the belly of the fish: 'There is no god but You; Glory be to You; indeed I have been among the wrongdoers.' No Muslim supplicates with it for anything except that it is answered for him."

**The third issue:** It is part of the Sunnah for one who begins eating to mention the name of Allah at his eating and drinking, and to praise Him at the end of it, following the example of the people of Paradise. In Sahih Muslim, from Anas ibn Malik, who said: the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Indeed Allah is pleased with the servant who eats a morsel and praises Him for it, or drinks a drink and praises Him for it."

**The fourth issue:** It is recommended for the one who supplicates to say at the end of his supplication, as the people of Paradise said: "And the last of their call is: 'All praise is due to Allah, Lord of the worlds.'" It is also good to recite the end of *al-Saffat* (see vol. 15, p. 140), for it combines the glorification of the Creator (*al-Bari'*) above what is attributed to Him, the greeting of peace upon the messengers, and the conclusion with praise to Allah, Lord of the worlds.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 10, verse 11:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And if Allah were to hasten for people the evil as they seek to hasten the good, their term would surely have been decreed for them﴾. In this there are three issues.

The first: His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿And if Allah were to hasten for people the evil﴾. It has been said: its meaning is that if Allah hastened punishment for people as they seek to hasten reward and good, they would die, because in the world they were created weak, whereas on the Day of Resurrection they are not like this, for on the Day of Resurrection they will be created for permanence. It has also been said: the meaning is that if Allah dealt with people in responding to what is disliked in the same way they wish to deal with Him in responding to what is good, He would destroy them, and this is the meaning of ﴿their term would surely have been decreed for them﴾. It has also been said that it is specific to the disbeliever, meaning: if Allah were to bring punishment upon the disbeliever for his disbelief just as He hastens for him the worldly good of wealth and children, He would hasten the decree of his term so that he would hasten the punishment of the Hereafter. This was said by Ibn Ishaq. Muqatil said: it is the saying of al-Nadr ibn al-Harith: "O Allah, if this is the truth from You, then rain down upon us stones from the sky." So if this had been hastened for them, they would have perished. Mujahid said: it was revealed concerning a man who, when angry, invokes curses upon himself, his property, or his child, saying: "O Allah, destroy him, O Allah, do not bless him in it, and curse him," or something similar. If that were answered as good is answered, their term would surely have been decreed. Thus the verse was revealed as a condemnation of a blameworthy trait found in some people, who supplicate for good while wanting its answer hastened; then bad character sometimes drives them to supplicate for evil, and if it were hastened for them, they would perish.

The second: There is difference concerning the answering of this kind of supplication. It is related from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "I asked Allah, mighty and majestic, not to answer the supplication of a beloved against his beloved." Shahr ibn Hawshab said: I read in some books that Allah, exalted, says to the angels assigned to the servant: "Do not record against My servant in a state of his distress anything, out of kindness from Allah, exalted, toward him." Some of them said: such supplication is sometimes answered, and they argued with the hadith of Jabir which Muslim related in his Sahih at the end of the book. Jabir said: We journeyed with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in the expedition of Batn Buwat [[Buwat (with its first letter vowelled with a damma): a mountain of the mountains of Juhayna in the region of Radwa (a mountain near Medina), the expedition of the Prophet (ﷺ) in the month of Rabi' al-Awwal in the second year of the Hijra, seeking Quraysh.]], and he was seeking al-Mujdi ibn Amr al-Juhani. The water-camel was passed around among us, five, six, or seven of us riding it in turn. The turn of a man from the Ansar came upon a water-camel of his, so he made it kneel and rode it, then urged it on, and it balked and hesitated somewhat. So he said to it: "Go, may Allah curse you!" The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: "Who is this who curses his camel?" He said: "I am, O Messenger of Allah." He said: "Dismount from it, and do not accompany us with one who is cursed. Do not invoke curses upon yourselves, do not invoke curses upon your children, and do not invoke curses upon your property, lest you coincide with a moment from Allah in which a gift is asked and He answers you." In another narration, not in Muslim's, that the Prophet (ﷺ) was on a journey when a man cursed his she-camel, and he said: "Where is the one who cursed his she-camel?" The man said: "I am here, O Messenger of Allah." He said: "Let her go away from you, for your request concerning her has been answered." This was mentioned by al-Halimi in Minhaj al-Din. "Sha'" is narrated with sin and shin, and it is a command to the camel meaning "go."

The third: His saying, may He be exalted, ﴿And if Allah were to hasten﴾. The scholars said: hastening (al-ta'jil) is from Allah, and seeking to hasten (al-isti'jal) is from the servant. Abu 'Ali said: both are from Allah, and in the speech there is an ellipsis, meaning: "And if Allah were to hasten for people the evil with a hastening like their seeking of the good," then he omitted "hastening" and put its description in its place, then he omitted its description and put the object of the preposition in its place. This is the view of al-Khalil and Sibawayh. According to the view of al-Akhfash and al-Farra', it is "as their seeking," then the kaf was omitted and the word put in the accusative. Al-Farra' said: just as you say "I struck Zayd a striking like yours," meaning "like your striking." Ibn 'Amir read "Liqudiya ilayhim ajaluhum" (with the passive form). This is a good reading, because it is connected to His saying: "And if Allah were to hasten for people the evil."

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So We leave those who do not expect to meet Us﴾, meaning: He does not hasten evil for them, for perhaps a repenting one among them will repent, or a believer will come forth from their loins.

﴿In their transgression they wander blindly﴾, meaning: they are bewildered. Al-tughyan is elevation and rising, and it has been discussed before in al-Baqara [[See vol. 1 p. 209.]]. It has also been said that the intended people in this verse are the people of Makkah, and that it was revealed when they said: ﴿O Allah, if this is the truth from You, then rain down upon us stones from the sky﴾ [al-Anfal: 32], as previously mentioned [[vol. 7 p. 398.]]. And Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 10, verse 12:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when harm touches man, he calls upon Us, lying on his side, or sitting, or standing﴾. It has been said: what is meant by "man" here is the disbeliever. It has been said: he is Abu Hudhayfah ibn al-Mughirah the polytheist, who is afflicted by hardship (al-ba'sa'), distress (al-shiddah) and suffering (al-jahd). "Calls upon Us, lying on his side" means: upon his side, lying down.

(Or sitting or standing): He intended all his states, because a person does not go beyond one of these three conditions. Some of them said: He began with the one lying down because, in most cases, harm affects him more severely, so he calls out more, and his effort is greater; then the one sitting, then the one standing.

(So when We remove from him his harm, he passes on) meaning: he continues in his disbelief, does not give thanks, and does not take heed. I say: this is the characteristic of many of the mixed-up monotheists: when well-being reaches them, they pass on in the sins they were committing. So the verse encompasses the disbeliever and others.

(As if he had never called upon Us). Al-Akhfash said: it is "ka'anna" (as if) in its heavy form, lightened, and the meaning is "ka'annahu" (as if he). He recited:

"Wai, ka'an man yakun lahu nashabun yuhabbab, wa man yaftaqir ya'ish 'aysha dhurr"
(Alas, as if one who has wealth is loved, and one who is poor lives a life of hardship.) [The verse is by Zayd ibn 'Amr ibn Nufayl; refer to Khizanat al-Adab, the seventy-eighth witness after the four hundredth.]

(Thus it was made attractive) meaning: just as this supplication was made attractive to him in times of trial, so was turning away made attractive to him in times of ease.

(It was made attractive to the extravagant) meaning: their deeds of disbelief and sins were made attractive to the polytheists. This making-attractive may be from Allah, and it may be from Satan, and his misguidance is his calling to disbelief.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 10, verse 13:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We destroyed the generations before you when they did wrong﴾. He means the past nations before the people of Makkah. We destroyed them.

(when they did wrong) That is, they disbelieved and associated partners with Allah.

(and their messengers came to them with clear proofs) That is, with manifest miracles and luminous evidences.

(and they were not going to believe) That is, We destroyed them because We knew that they would not believe. It warns the disbelievers of Makkah of the punishment of the past nations; that is, We are able to destroy these people for their denial of Muhammad (ﷺ), but We give them respite because We know that among them is one who will believe, or that one who will believe will come forth from their loins. This verse refutes the people of misguidance who say that guidance and faith are created [by Allah in a way that bypasses human choice]. It has also been said: the meaning of "and they were not going to believe" is that He requited them for their disbelief by sealing their hearts, and what supports this is His saying: ﴿Thus do We recompense the criminal people﴾.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 10, verse 14:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Then We made you successors (khala'if)﴾. It is a two-object construction (maf'ulan). Al-Khala'if is the plural of khalifah (successor, vicegerent), and it has already been discussed at the end of "al-An'am" [[See vol. 7, p. 158.]]. That is, We made you inhabitants of the earth. ﴿After them﴾ means after the generations that were destroyed. ﴿That We might see﴾ (li-nazhura) is in the subjunctive by the particle of purpose (lam kay), and its parallels and similar cases have already been discussed. That is, so that there would occur from you what makes you deserving of reward and punishment, while He has always known it in the unseen. It was also said: He deals with you in the manner of one who tests, to manifest justice. And it was also said: the "seeing" refers to the messengers, meaning: that Our messengers and Our friends might see how your deeds are. And "how" (kayfa) is in the accusative by His saying "you do" (ta'malun), because the interrogative has the front position in the sentence, so what precedes it cannot govern it.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 10, verse 15:

There are three issues in this verse.

The first: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿When Our clear revelations are recited to them﴾. "Tutla" means "recited," and "bayyinat" (clear) is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (hal), meaning clear, with no ambiguity or obscurity in them.

(﴿Those who do not expect to meet Us say﴾) meaning: those who do not fear the Day of Resurrection and reckoning, and do not hope for reward. Qatadah said: this refers to the polytheists of Makkah.

(﴿Bring a Qur'an other than this, or change it﴾). The difference between changing it (tabdil) and bringing something other than it (al-ityan bi-ghayrihi) is that changing it cannot be done alongside it, whereas bringing something other than it may be done alongside it. There are three interpretations of their request:

The first: they asked him to transform promise into threat and threat into promise, and lawful into unlawful and unlawful into lawful. This was said by Ibn Jarir al-Tabari.

The second: they asked him to remove from the Qur'an the criticism of their gods and the mockery of their intellects. This was said by Ibn 'Isa.

The third: they asked him to remove from it the mention of resurrection and rising again. This was said by al-Zajjaj.

The second issue: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: It is not for me﴾, meaning: say, O Muhammad, it is not for me ﴿to change it on my own accord﴾, that is, from my own self and by my own opinion, just as it is not for me to reject it or deny it.

(﴿I follow only what is revealed to me﴾) meaning: I follow only what I recite to you of promise and threat, prohibition and permission, and command and prohibition. Some have used this verse to argue against abrogating the Book by the Sunnah, since He, exalted is He, said: "Say: It is not for me to change it on my own accord." However, this argument is far-fetched, for the verse was revealed concerning the polytheists' demand for something like the Qur'an in its wording, and the Messenger (ﷺ) was not able to do that. They did not ask him to change the ruling without the wording. Moreover, what the Messenger (ﷺ) says, when it is revelation, is not from his own self but from Allah, exalted is He.

The third issue: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, I fear, if I disobey my Lord﴾, meaning: if I oppose Him by changing or altering it, or by failing to act upon it.

(﴿The punishment of a tremendous day﴾) meaning: the Day of Resurrection.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 10, verse 16:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: "If God had willed, I would not have recited it to you, nor would He have made you aware of it."﴾ That is, if God had willed, He would not have sent me to you so that I recited the Qur'an to you, and God would not have informed you of it or told you about it. It is said: "I knew (daraytu) the thing, and God made me know it (adrani Allahu bihi)," and "I knew it (daraytuhu)" and "I knew of it (daraytu bihi)." In the word al-dirayah (knowledge) there is also the meaning of deception (al-khatl), and from it comes "daraytu al-rajul," meaning I deceived the man. For this reason al-Dari (the Knower) is not applied to God, the Exalted; and also, there is no scriptural basis (tawqif) for it.

Ibn Kathir recited: "wa-la-adrakum bihi" without an alif between the lam and the hamza. The meaning is: If God had willed, He would have made you know of it without my reciting it to you. Here the lam is the lam of emphasis (lam al-ta'kid) that entered upon the alif of af'ala (the form of the verb). Ibn 'Abbas and al-Hasan recited: "wa-la adratukum bihi," with the yā' converted into an alif (in the sense that the original is "adraytukum"), according to the dialect of the Banu 'Uqayl. The poet said:

"La'amruka ma akhsha al-tasa'lka ma baqa ... 'ala al-ardi qaysiyyun yasuqu al-aba'ira"

And another said:

"Ala adhanat ahla al-yamamati Ta'iyyun ... bi-harbin ka-nasati al-aghharri al-mushahhari"

Abu Hatim said: I heard al-Asma'i say: I asked Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala': "Is there any justification for the recitation of al-Hasan, 'wa-la adratukum bihi'?" He said: "No." Abu 'Ubayd said: There is no justification for the recitation of al-Hasan, "wa-la adratukum bihi," except error (ghalat). Al-Nahhas said: The meaning of Abu 'Ubayd's words "there is no justification" is, if God wills, that it is an error, because it is said "daraytu," meaning I knew, and "adraytu ghayri," meaning I made another know; and it is said "daratu," meaning I pushed away, so error may occur between "daraytu" and "daratu." Abu Hatim said: What al-Hasan intends, as far as I suppose, is "wa-la adraytukum bihi," and he changed the yā' to an alif according to the dialect of the Banu al-Harith ibn Ka'b, who change the yā' to an alif when the letter before it has a fatha, like: ﴿Indeed, these two are certainly sorcerers﴾ [Ta-Ha: 63]. (See vol. 11, p. 215 onward.) Al-Mahdawi said: As for the one who recited "adra'tukum," its basis is that the original of the hamza is a yā'; the original is "adraytukum," then the yā' was changed to an alif even though it was sakin, as in "Yays" for "yay's" and "Ta'i" for "Tay'," then the alif was changed to a hamza, according to the dialect of those who say "al-'a'lam" for "al-'alam" and "al-kha'tam" for "al-khatam." Al-Nahhas said: This is an error. The transmission from al-Hasan is "wa-la adra'tukum" with a hamza, and Abu Hatim and others have stated that it is without a hamza. It is possible that it comes from "dara'tu," meaning I pushed away, that is: nor would I have commanded you to push away and thus abandon disbelief in the Qur'an.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, I have remained among you a lifetime before it﴾. "A lifetime" (*'umuran*) is an adverbial accusative (zarf), meaning a span of time, which is forty years.

(*Min qablihi*) That is, before the Qur'an, you know me for truthfulness and trustworthiness; I do not read or write, then I came to you with the miracles.

(*Afala ta'qilun*) That this cannot be except from God, not from me. It is also said: the meaning of "I remained among you a lifetime" is: I remained among you through the period of my youth, not disobeying God; will you now, after I have reached forty years, wish me to oppose the command of God and change what He reveals to me? Qatadah said: I remained among them forty years, and he stayed two years seeing the dreams of the prophets, and he passed away ﷺ at the age of sixty-two.

This is an interrogative used to express denial: there is no one more unjust than the one who fabricates a lie against God, alters His speech, and adds to it something He did not reveal. Likewise, there is no one more unjust than you, if you deny the Qur'an, fabricate a lie against God, and say, "This is not His speech." This is among the things the Messenger (ﷺ) was commanded to say to them. It was also said: it is from God's own speech, beginning the statement. And it was said: the one who fabricates (al-muftari) is the polytheist, while those who deny the signs (al-mukadhdhibun bil-ayat) are the People of the Book. ﴿Indeed, the criminals will not succeed.﴾

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 10, verse 18:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And they worship besides Allah that which can neither harm them nor benefit them﴾. He means the idols.

(And they say, "These are our intercessors with Allah.") This is the utmost ignorance on their part, for they expect intercession in the future from one who has neither benefit nor harm in the present. It was also said: "our intercessors" means that they will intercede for us with Allah regarding the setting right of our livelihoods in this world.

(Say, "Do you inform Allah of what He does not know in the heavens or on the earth?") The recitation of the common readers is "tunabbi'ūna" with a doubled ba' (tashdid). Abu al-Sammal al-'Adawi recited "atunbi'ūna Allah" without the doubling, from anba'a yunbi'u. The recitation of the common readers is from nabba'a yunabbi'u tanbi'ah, and both have one meaning, which His saying, may He be exalted, brings together: ﴿Who informed you of this? He said: The All-Knowing, the All-Aware informed me﴾ [al-Tahrim: 3]. That is: Do you inform Allah that He has a partner in His dominion or an intercessor without His permission, while Allah does not know of any partner for Himself in the heavens or on the earth, because He has no partner, and therefore He does not know of one? A parallel to this is His saying: ﴿Or do you inform Him of what He does not know in the earth?﴾ [al-Ra'd: 33]. Then He declared Himself free of and exalted above association, saying: "Glory be to Him, and exalted is He above what they associate." That is, He is far too great to have a partner.

It was also said: the meaning is that they worship what does not hear, does not see, and does not discern, [in some manuscripts: "what does not intercede nor help"] "and they say, 'These are our intercessors with Allah'," so they lie. Is it possible for you to inform Him of what He does not know? Glory be to Him and exalted is He above what they associate!

Hamzah and al-Kisa'i recited "tushrikūn" with the ta' (second person), and this is the choice of Abu 'Ubayd. The rest read it with the ya' (third person).

The Qur'an's commentary on this has already been given in *al-Baqarah* [[See vol. 3, p. 30.]], so its meaning need not be repeated here. Al-Zajjaj said: they are the Arabs, who were upon polytheism. It was also said: every child is born upon the *fitrah* (the innate disposition to recognise God), and then they differed upon reaching maturity. ﴿And had it not been for a word that preceded from your Lord, it would have been decided between them concerning that wherein they differ﴾. This refers to *al-qada' wa'l-qadar* (divine decree and predestination). That is, were it not for what had already been determined in His judgement, that He would not judge between them concerning what they differed over, with reward and punishment, except on the Day of Resurrection, it would have been decided between them in this world. So He would have admitted the believers to Paradise for their deeds and the disbelievers to the Fire for their disbelief. But a fixed term had already been set by God, along with His knowledge of their conduct, so He made their appointed time the Resurrection. This was said by al-Hasan. Abu Rawq said: "it would have been decided between them" means He would have established the Hour against them. It was also said: it would have been finished with their destruction. Al-Kalbi said: "the word" is that God delayed this community, so He would not destroy them with punishment in this world until the Day of Resurrection. Had it not been for this delay, it would have been decided between them by the descent of punishment or by the establishment of the Hour. The verse is a consolation to the Prophet (ﷺ) regarding the delay of punishment for those who disbelieved in him. It was also said: the preceding word is that He does not seize anyone except with a proof, which is the sending of messengers, as He said: ﴿And We never punish until We have sent a messenger﴾ [Al-Isra: 15]. It was also said: the word is His saying, "My mercy has preceded My wrath," and were it not for that, He would not have delayed the disobedient until repentance. Ibn Isa read "liquḍiya" with a fatḥah (i.e., *لقضي* pronounced with a short "a" on the first letter, the verb in the passive form).

It is referring to the people of Makkah: that is, "Why has no sign (ayah), i.e. a miracle other than this miracle, been sent down to him, so that He would make the mountains gold for us, and he would have a house of ornament, and He would bring back to life for us those of our fathers who have died." Al-Dahhak said: "A staff like the staff of Musa."

(So say: The unseen belongs only to Allah) — i.e., say, O Muhammad, that the sending down of the sign is something unseen.

(So wait) — i.e., be patient and watch.

(Indeed, I am with you among those who wait) — for its descent. It was also said: "Wait for Allah's judgment between us, by making the truth manifest over the falsifier."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 10, verse 21:

It refers to the disbelievers of Makkah.

(Mercy after some adversity has touched them) It was said: prosperity after hardship, and abundance after drought.

(Then they have a plot against Our verses) That is, mockery and denial. The answer to His saying, "And when We let them taste...": "then they have a plot" according to the opinion of al-Khalil (ibn Ahmad al-Farahidi) and Sibawayh. "Say: Allah is swifter in plotting" is a subject and predicate. "Makran" (in plotting) is in the sense of specification (tamyiz/bayan), meaning: swifter in punishment as a requital for their plotting; that is, what comes to them of punishment is swifter in destroying them than the plotting they have committed.

(Indeed Our messengers record what you plot) By "messengers" is meant the guardian angels (al-hafazah). The common reading is "tamkurun" with the ta' (addressing you directly). Ya'qub, in the transmission of Ruways, and Abu 'Amr, in the transmission of Harun al-'Ataki, read "yamkurun" with the ya', in accordance with His saying: "then they have a plot against Our verses." It was said: Abu Sufyan said, "We have suffered drought, so pray for us; if you give us rain, we will believe you." So they were given rain through his supplication (ﷺ), but they did not believe. This is their plotting.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿It is He who enables you to travel on land and sea, until when you are in the ships and they sail with them﴾. That is, He carries you on land upon beasts and at sea upon ships. Al-Kalbi said: He protects you while you travel. The verse includes an enumeration of blessings in the matter in which people are established, namely riding beasts and the sea.
