Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 10, verse 24:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, the example of the worldly life is like water which We sent down from the sky﴾. The meaning of the verse is comparison and parable, i.e., the description of the worldly life in its transience, its passing away, the smallness of its worth, and the pleasures found in it, is like water, i.e., like [the example of] water. The kaf (the "like" particle) is in the position of raf' (nominative). Further elucidation of this comparison will come in Surat al-Kahf, God willing [see vol. 10, p. 412]. "Which We sent down from the sky" is a qualifier of "water."

(So the vegetation of the earth mingled with it) It is narrated from Nafi' that he paused at "fa-ikhtalata" (so it mingled), meaning the water mingled with the earth, and then began with "bihi nabatu al-ard" (by it the plants of the earth), meaning by the water the plants of the earth [came forth], so that they produced various colors of vegetation. On this reading, "nabat" is a new beginning (mubtada'). According to those who do not pause at "fa-ikhtalata," "nabat" is in the nominative case, governed by "ikhtalata," meaning the vegetation mingled with the rain, i.e., it drank from it, so it became moist, fine, and green. Ikhtilat (mingling) is the interpenetration of one thing with another.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿of what men and livestock eat﴾: from grains, fruits, and herbs.

(And livestock) from pasture, straw, and barley.

(Until, when the earth took on its adornment) i.e., its beauty and finery. Zukhruf is the perfection of a thing's beauty, and from this gold is called zukhruf.

(And was adorned) i.e., with grains, fruits, and flowers. The original form is tazayyanat; the taa' was assimilated into the zay and an alif of connection (alif al-wasl) was brought in, because an assimilated letter stands for two letters, the first of which is quiescent, and a quiescent letter cannot be begun with. Ibn Mas'ud and Ubayy ibn Ka'b read "wa-tazayyanat" according to the original form. Al-Hasan, al-A'raj, and Abu al-'Aliyah read "wa-azyanat," meaning it brought adornment upon itself, i.e., the produce and the crops; the verb was kept in its original form, for had it been altered it would have said "wa-azanat." Awf ibn Abi Jamilah al-A'rabi said: "Our shaykhs read 'wa-azyannat,' its pattern being according to isswaddat." In the narration of al-Muqaddami it is "wa-azzayanat," and its original form is tazayanat, its pattern being taqa'asat, then it was assimilated. Al-Sha'bi and Qatadah read "wa-azyanat" in the pattern of af'alat. Abu 'Uthman al-Nahdi read "wa-azyanat" in the pattern of if'alat; and from him also "wa-azyanat" in the pattern of if'alat(?) and "azyani'at" with a hamza, three readings.

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿and its people think that they have power over it﴾, i.e., they are certain.

(That they are able over it) i.e., over its harvesting and benefiting from it. He reports about the earth, while the meaning is the vegetation, since it is understood and is part of it. It was said: it refers to the produce; and it was said: it refers to the adornment.

(There comes to it Our command) i.e., Our punishment, or We command its destruction.

(By night or by day) two adverbial expressions of time.

(So We made it a harvest) two objects, i.e., mowed down and cut off, with nothing remaining in it. He said "hasidan" and did not make it feminine because it is a fa'il in the sense of maf'ul. Abu 'Ubayd said: al-hasid is that which is uprooted.

(As if it had not flourished yesterday) i.e., it had not been inhabited, from ghana, when one dwells in a place and makes it prosperous. Al-maghani in the language are the dwellings that people inhabit. Qatadah said: "ka'an lam tana'am" (as if it had not been pleasant). Labid said:

*"And I dwelt a long while before the course of Dahis, had there been eternity for the stubborn soul."* [[al-sabt: a span of time. Dahis: the name of a horse.]]

The common reading is "taghna" with the taa', because the earth is feminine. Qatadah read "yaghna" with the yaa', referring it to the adornment: just as this crop perishes, so too the world.

(We detail the signs) i.e., We make them clear.

(For a people who reflect) upon the signs of God.

The commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 10, verse 25:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And Allah calls to the Abode of Peace﴾. When He mentioned the description of this abode, which is the abode of the world, He described the Hereafter, saying: Indeed, Allah does not call you to gather the world, but He calls you to obedience so that you may arrive at the Abode of Peace, that is, Paradise. Qatadah and al-Hasan said: "al-Salam" is Allah, and His abode is Paradise, and Paradise is called the Abode of Peace because whoever enters it is safe from afflictions. Among His names, glory be to Him, is "al-Salam," and we have explained this in (al-Kitab al-Asna fi Sharh Asma' Allah al-Husna, The Most Excellent Book on the Explanation of the Names of Allah, the Most Beautiful). It will come in Surah al-Hashr [[See vol. 18, p. 45.]], God willing. It was also said: the meaning is "And Allah calls to the Abode of Safety." Al-Salam and al-Salamah have the same meaning, like al-Rada' and al-Radha'ah, as said by al-Zajjaj. The poet said:

"Umm Bakr greets you with safety, / And is there for you, after your people, any peace?"

It was also said: He intended "And Allah calls to the Abode of Greeting," because its people receive greeting and peace from Allah, and likewise from the angels. Al-Hasan said: Peace does not cease for the people of Paradise; it is their greeting, as He said: ﴿And their greeting therein is peace﴾ [Yunus: 10]. Yahya ibn Mu'adh said: O son of Adam, Allah has called you to the Abode of Peace, so look from where you respond to Him. If you respond to Him from your worldly life, you will enter it; and if you respond to Him from your grave, you will be prevented from it. Ibn Abbas said: The gardens are seven: the Abode of Majesty, the Abode of Peace, Jannat 'Adn, Jannat al-Ma'wa, Jannat al-Khuld, Jannat al-Firdaws, and Jannat al-Na'im.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And He guides whom He wills to a straight path﴾. He generalized the call to show His proof, and specified guidance to indicate His independence from His creation. As for "the straight path," it was said to be the Book of Allah. Ali ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him) narrated this, saying: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "The straight path is the Book of Allah, the Exalted." It was also said to be Islam, narrated by al-Nawwas ibn Sam'an from the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ). It was said to be the Truth, as said by Qatadah and Mujahid. It was also said to be the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) and his two companions after him, Abu Bakr and Umar (may Allah be pleased with them both).

Jabir ibn Abdullah narrated: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) came out one day and said: "I saw in a dream as if Jibril was at my head and Mika'il was at my feet. One of them said to his companion: Strike a parable for him. He said to him: Listen, may your ears hear; understand, may your heart understand. Your parable and the parable of your community is like that of a king who acquired a house, then built a room in it, then prepared a feast in it, then sent a messenger calling the people to his food. Some of them answered the messenger, and some of them left him. So Allah is the King, the House is Islam, the Room is Paradise, and you, O Muhammad, are the Messenger. Whoever answers you enters Islam, whoever enters Islam enters Paradise, and whoever enters Paradise eats of what is in it." Then the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) recited: ﴿And He guides whom He wills to a straight path﴾ [[This verse and the sentence before it are not in manuscripts B, K, H, and Y.]]. Then Qatadah and Mujahid recited: ﴿And Allah calls to the Abode of Peace﴾.

This verse is a clear proof in refuting the Qadariyya (the sect that denies divine predestination), because they said: Allah guided all creation to the straight path. But Allah said: ﴿And He guides whom He wills to a straight path﴾. So they rejected the texts of the Qur'an.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 10, verse 26:

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿For those who did good is the best reward, and more﴾. It is related from the hadith of Anas, who said: The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was asked about His saying, "and more," and he said: "For those who did good deeds in this world there is the best reward, which is Paradise, and the more is looking at the Noble Face of Allah." This is also the saying of Abu Bakr al-Siddiq and of Ali ibn Abi Talib in one narration; and of Hudhayfah, Ubadah ibn al-Samit, Ka'b ibn Ujrah, Abu Musa, Suhayb and Ibn Abbas in one narration. It is also the saying of a group of the Followers, and it is the sound view on this matter.

Muslim related in his Sahih from Suhayb, from the Prophet (ﷺ), that he said: "When the people of Paradise enter Paradise, Allah, blessed and exalted, says: 'Do you want anything more that I should give you?' They say: 'Have You not made our faces bright? Have You not admitted us to Paradise and saved us from the Fire?' He said: Then the veil is lifted, and they are given nothing more beloved to them than looking at their Lord, Mighty and Majestic." (In another narration he then recited: "For those who did good is the best reward, and more.")

Al-Nasa'i also transmitted it from Suhayb, who said: It was said to the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ): "This verse, 'For those who did good is the best reward, and more'?" He said: "When the people of Paradise have entered Paradise and the people of the Fire have entered the Fire, a caller will call out: 'O people of Paradise, you have a promise with Allah which He wishes to fulfil for you.' They will say: 'Has He not made our faces bright, made our scales heavy, and protected us from the Fire?' He said: Then the veil is lifted and they look at Him; by Allah, Allah has given them nothing more beloved to them than looking, nor more delightful to their eyes." Ibn al-Mubarak also transmitted it in his Daqa'iq from Abu Musa al-Ash'ari as a statement of his own (mawquf). We have mentioned it in the book al-Tadhkirah, and we mentioned there the meaning of the lifting of the veil, and praise be to Allah.

Al-Tirmidhi al-Hakim Abu Abd Allah, may Allah have mercy on him, transmitted: Ali ibn Hujr narrated to us, al-Walid ibn Muslim narrated to us, from Zuhayr, from Abu al-Aliyah, from Ubayy ibn Ka'b, who said: I asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about the two increases in the Book of Allah, in His saying, "For those who did good is the best reward, and more." He said: "Looking at the Face of the Most Merciful." And about His saying: ﴿And We sent him to a hundred thousand or more﴾ [al-Saffat: 147], he said: "Twenty thousand."

It has also been said that the increase is that a good deed is multiplied tenfold up to more than that; this is related from Ibn Abbas. It is related from Ali ibn Abi Talib, may Allah be pleased with him: the increase is one chamber of pearl with four thousand doors. Mujahid said: "The best" is one good deed like one good deed, and the increase is forgiveness from Allah and His pleasure. Abd al-Rahman ibn Zayd ibn Aslam said: "The best" is Paradise, and the increase is what Allah gives them in this world of His bounty, which He does not reckon against them on the Day of Resurrection. Abd al-Rahman ibn Sabit said: "The best" is glad tidings, and the increase is looking at the Noble Face of Allah. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Faces that Day will be radiant, looking toward their Lord﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 22–23]. Yazid ibn Shajarah said: The increase is that a cloud passes over the people of Paradise and rains upon them from every rare thing they have not seen, and says: "O people of Paradise, what do you want me to rain upon you?" They want nothing but that it rains it upon them.

It has also been said: the increase is that not a moment of a day of the days of this world passes over them without seventy thousand angels coming around the dwelling of each one of them, with every angel bearing gifts from Allah that the companion does not have; they have never seen the like of those gifts. Glory be to the All-Encompassing, the All-Knowing, the Rich, the Praiseworthy, the Exalted, the Great, the Mighty, the Powerful, the Good, the Merciful, the Disposer, the Wise, the Subtle, the Generous, He whose power is not exhausted.

It has been said: "those who did good" means in their dealings with people, "the best" means their intercession, and the increase is Allah's permission for it and His acceptance of it.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And no dust nor humiliation will cover them﴾. It has been said: its meaning is "reach" (yalhaq); from this comes the saying "a youth who is murahiq" when he has reached the men. It has also been said: "cover" (ya'lu); and it has been said: "overwhelm" (yaghsha); the meanings are close. "Qatar" means dust. "Nor humiliation" means abasement, as it reaches the people of the Fire; that is, no dust will reach them on their gathering to Allah, and no humiliation will overwhelm them. Abu Ubaydah recited for al-Farazdaq:

Crowned with the mantle of kingship, followed by a wave, above which you see banners and dust (qatara).

Al-Hasan read "qatr" with a sukun on the ta'. Qatar, qatarah and qatrah have one meaning, as al-Nahhas said. The singular of qatar is qatarah, and from it is the verse: ﴿Darkness will cover them﴾ [Abasa: 41], meaning dust will cover them. It has also been said: qatar is gloom and dejection. Ibn Abbas said: qatar is the blackness of faces. Ibn Bahr said: it is the smoke of the Fire, and from it comes "qutar al-qidr" (the steam of the cooking pot). Ibn Abi Layla said: it is the distance of their gaze from their Lord, Mighty and Majestic.

I say: this view is open to question, for Allah, Mighty and Majestic, says: ﴿Indeed, those for whom the best has already preceded from Us, they will be kept far from it﴾ up to His saying: ﴿The greatest terror will not grieve them﴾ [al-Anbiya': 101–103]. In other verses He says: ﴿And no fear will be upon them, nor will they grieve﴾ [al-Baqarah: 62], and He says: ﴿Indeed, those who say, "Our Lord is Allah," and then remain steadfast, the angels descend upon them: "Do not fear and do not grieve"﴾ [Fussilat: 30], and the verse. This is general, so it does not change by Allah's grace at any station, neither before the looking nor after it; the face of the doer of good is not darkened by blackness of sorrow or grief, and nothing of the smoke of Hell or anything else overtakes it.

﴿And as for those whose faces are made bright, they will be in Allah's mercy, therein they will abide forever﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 107].

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 10, verse 27:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And those who earned evil deeds﴾, i.e., committed sins. It is also said: [it means] association of partners with God (shirk).

(The recompense of an evil deed is its like) "Recompense" (jaza') is in the nominative, being the subject (mubtada'), and its predicate (khabar) is "its like" (bimithliha). Ibn Kaysan said: the ba' (bi-) is superfluous (za'idah), and the meaning is: the recompense of an evil deed is its like. It is also said: the ba' together with what follows it is the predicate, and it is connected to an omitted element that has taken its place, and the meaning is: the recompense of an evil deed is one that is in accordance with its like, as when you say: "I am only with you" (innama ana bika), meaning: "I am only one who is with you." It is permissible for it to be connected to "recompense," the sense being: "the recompense of an evil deed by its like is what is due," so the predicate of the subject is omitted. It is also permissible for "recompense" to be nominative by the supposition of: "then for them is the recompense of an evil deed," which is like His saying: ﴿So a number of other days﴾ [al-Baqarah: 184], i.e., "then upon him is a number [of days]," and similar. On this reading the ba' is connected to an omitted element, as if he said: "for them is a recompense of an evil deed established by its like," or it may be emphatic (muakkidah) or superfluous (za'idah). The meaning of this equivalence (mithliyyah) is that this recompense is something considered equal to their sins; that is, they are not wronged, and the act of the Lord [exalted is His power and majestic is His affair] is not dependent on any cause.

(And humiliation will cover them) i.e., disgrace and ignominy will overtake them.

(They will have no protector from God) i.e., from the punishment of God.

(From anyone to save them) i.e., one who will prevent it from them.

(As if their faces had been covered) i.e., clothed.

(With pieces of the night, dark) "Qit'an" is the plural of qit'ah (piece). On this reading, "muzlimān" (dark) is a circumstantial qualifier (hal) of "al-layl" (the night), i.e., their faces were covered with pieces of the night in the state of its darkness. Al-Kisa'i and Ibn Kathir read "qit'an" with the ta' sukun (qit'an), so "muzlimān" on this reading is a descriptive adjective (na't), and it is permissible for it to be a circumstantial qualifier of "al-layl." Al-qit' is the name of what is cut off and falls. Ibn al-Sikkit said: al-qit' is a portion of the night. It will come in Surah Hud, God willing, exalted is He.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 10, verse 28:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And [mention] the Day when We will gather them all together﴾. That is, We will assemble them, and al-hashr (gathering) means al-jam' (assembling). "Jami'an" (all together) is a ḥal (circumstantial accusative, describing the state of the subject at the time of the action).

(Then We will say to those who associated [others with Allah]) That is, those who took partners alongside Allah.

(Stay in your place) That is, remain and hold firm in your place; stand in your positions.

(You and your partners) And this is a threat (wa'id).

(Then We will separate them) That is, We will divide and sever what had existed between them of connection in the world. It is said: zayyaltuhu fa-tazayyala, meaning "I separated him and he was separated." It is on the pattern fa''altu, because you say its verbal noun is tazyil; had it been fay'altu, you would say zaylah. Al-muzayalah means parting (al-mufaraqah). It is said: zayalahu Allahu muzayalatan wa ziyalan, when Allah parted him from it. Al-tazayul means separation (al-tabayun). Al-Farra' said: Some of them read "fa-zayalna baynahum" (with the alif). It is said: la uzayilu fulanan, meaning "I do not part from so-and-so," that is, I do not leave him. But if you say la uzawiluhu (with the waw), it has a different meaning: it means "I do not deceive him" (la ukhatiluhu).

(And their partners will say) By "the partners" are meant the angels. It is also said: the devils. It is also said: the idols, and Allah will give them speech, so this dialogue takes place between them. That is because they will claim against the devils who were obeyed and the idols that were worshipped that they had commanded them to worship them, and they will say: "We did not worship you until you commanded us." Mujahid said: Allah will give speech to the idols, and they will say: "We were not aware that you were worshipping us, nor did we command you to worship us." If the partners are taken to mean the devils, then the meaning is that they say this in bewilderment, or they say it falsely and as a stratagem for deliverance. Something like this may also occur tomorrow, even if knowledge becomes necessary (ma'arif darurriyyah).

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 10, verse 29:

God's saying: ﴿So God suffices as a witness between us and you﴾. "Shahidan" (as a witness) is an object (maf'ul), meaning: God suffices as a witness. Or it is a specification (tamyiz), meaning: rely on Him as a witness between us and you, if we ever commanded you to this or were pleased with it from you.

(﴿If we were﴾) meaning, we were not, ﴿of your worship unaware﴾, except as those unaware who do not hear, do not see, and do not understand, because we were inanimate objects with no spirit in us.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 10, verse 30:

Allah's saying: ﴿Hunalika﴾ ("at that place" / "there") is in the accusative position as an adverb of time (zarf).

(Tabluu) means: at that time. "Tabluu" means: tadhuqu (experiences/tastes). Al-Kalbi said: ta'lamu (knows). Mujahid said: takhtabiru (tests).

(Kullu nafsin ma aslafat) means: the recompense for what it did and sent forward. It was also said: tusallimu, that is, every soul hands over to its rightful owners, without its own choice, the rights that are upon it. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i read "tatlu," meaning: every soul reads its book that was written for it. It was also said: "tatlu" means tatba'u (follows), that is, every soul follows what it sent forward in the world; this was said by al-Suddi. From this is the saying of the poet:

Indeed the doubter follows the doubter ... just as you have seen the wolf follow the wolf.

Allah's saying: ﴿Wa-rudduu ila Allahi mawlahumu al-haqq﴾ is in the genitive case (bi-l-khafd) as a substitute (badal) or an attribute (sifah). It is permissible to put "al-haqq" in the accusative in three ways: the meaning would be "they are returned as truth," then the alif and lam is brought (i.e., the word is made definite). It is also permissible that the meaning is: "their mawla (master) truly, not what they worship besides Him." The third way is that it is a praise, meaning: I mean the Truth. It is also permissible that "al-haqq" be in the nominative, and the meaning would be: "their mawla is the Truth," as an inceptive and predicate, and a break from what precedes, "not what they associate besides Him." He described Himself, glorified is He, as the Truth because the truth is from Him, just as He described Himself as Just because justice is from Him; that is, every justice and truth comes from Him. Ibn Abbas said: "mawlahum bil-haqq" means the one who recompenses them with truth.

(Wa-dalla 'anhum) means: it perished/was lost to them.

(Ma kanu yaftarun) "Yaftarun" is in the nominative position and is in the sense of a verbal noun (masdar), meaning: their fabrication. If it is asked: how did He say "they are returned to Allah, their true Master," when He had informed that the disbelievers have no mawla? It is answered: He is not their mawla in victory and support, but He is their mawla in provision and the pouring out of blessings.

The purpose of the thrust of this passage is to refute the polytheists and to establish the proof against them. Whoever among them acknowledges it, the proof is evident against him. Whoever does not acknowledge it, it is affirmed against him that these heavens and this earth must have a Creator, and no sensible person disputes this. This is close to the level of what is self-evident (ḍarūrah, that which is known necessarily without need for proof).

"From the sky" means by rain, and "and the earth" means by plants.

(Or who controls hearing and sight?) That is, who created them and brought them into being for you.

(And who brings the living out of the dead?) That is, brings forth plants from the earth, a human from a drop of semen, the ear of grain from the seed, a bird from the egg, and the believer from the disbeliever.

(And who arranges the affair?) That is, who decrees it and decides it.

(They will say, "Allah.") Because they used to believe that the Creator is Allah. Or: they will say, "It is Allah," if they reflect and are fair. (Then say) to them, O Muhammad.

(Will you not then fear Him?) That is, will you not fear His punishment and His vengeance in this world and the Hereafter.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 10, verse 32 (part 1 of 2):

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So that is Allah, your Lord, the Truth. Then what is there after the truth except error?﴾ In this verse there are eight issues.

The first: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿So that is Allah, your Lord, the Truth﴾, meaning: this One who does these things is your true Lord, not what you associate with Him. "Then what is there after the truth" — "dha" (ذا) is superfluous (ṣilah), meaning: what is there after the worship of the true God, when you abandon His worship, except error (ḍalāl)? Some of the early scholars said: the apparent meaning of this verse indicates that what lies beyond Allah is error, because its beginning is "So that is Allah, your Lord, the Truth" and its end is "Then what is there after the truth except error." This concerns belief and disbelief, not deeds. Some of them said: disbelief is the covering of the truth, and everything that is not the truth follows this course; so the forbidden is error and the permitted is guidance, since it is Allah who permits and forbids. The correct view is the first, because before "Say: Who provides for you from the heaven and the earth?" and then He said "So that is Allah, your Lord, the Truth," meaning: this is the One who provided for you, and all of this is His action. "Your Lord, the Truth" means the One who deserves divinity and merits worship; and when that is so, associating anything else with Him is error and not truth.

The second: Our scholars said: this verse rules that there is no third station between truth and falsehood in this matter, which is the Oneness of Allah, exalted is He, and likewise the matter is in its counterparts, namely the issues of the fundamentals (uṣūl), in which the truth lies on one side only. This is because the discussion concerning them is only about enumerating the existence of an essence and how it is. This is unlike the issues of the branches (furūʿ), concerning which Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿For each of you We have appointed a law and a method﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 48]. And his peace be upon him said: (The lawful is clear and the unlawful is clear, and between them are matters that are unclear). The discussion in the branches concerns rulings that supervene upon the existence of an established essence, about which there is no disagreement; disagreement is only about the rulings connected to it.

The third: It is established from ʿĀ'ishah, may Allah be pleased with her, that the Prophet ﷺ, whenever he stood for prayer in the depth of the night, would say: (O Allah, to You belongs praise) — the hadith. And in it: (You are the Truth, and Your promise is true, and Your word is true, and meeting You is true, and Paradise is true, and the Fire is true, and the Hour is true, and the prophets are true, and Muhammad is true) — the hadith. So his saying "You are the Truth" means the Necessarily Existent, and its root is from "ḥaqqa al-shay'" meaning it was established and became obligatory. This description applies to Allah, exalted is He, in reality, since His existence is from Himself: non-existence did not precede it and non-existence does not befall it, whereas everything else to which this name is applied is preceded by non-existence, may be subject to the coming of non-existence, and its existence is from its Originator, not from itself. In accordance with this meaning, the most truthful word spoken by a poet is the word of Labid:

"Surely everything other than Allah is vain (bāṭil)."

**Second**, the statement of Allah the Exalted, ﴿Everything will perish except His Face. His is the command, and to Him you will be returned﴾ [Al-Qasas: 88], refers to this. [See vol. 13, p. 223.]

**Fourth**: The opposition of truth (al-haqq) to error (al-dalal) is known both linguistically and in the Sharia, as in this verse. Likewise, the opposition of truth to falsehood (al-batil) is known linguistically and in the Sharia. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿That is because Allah is the Truth, and what they invoke besides Him is falsehood﴾ [Luqman: 30]. [See vol. 12, p. 91.]

The essential meaning of *dalal* is departing from the truth, taken from *dalal al-tariq* (losing the way), which means deviating from its direction. Ibn Arafa said: "*Dalala* among the Arabs is following a course other than the straight path. It is said: *dalla 'an al-tariq* (he strayed from the road), and *adalla al-shay'* (he lost the thing) when he wasted it." In the Sharia, it is specifically used for deviation from correctness in belief rather than in deeds. It is strange that it is also used to express not knowing the Truth, may He be glorified, when heedlessness is its opposite and ignorance or doubt does not accompany this lack. The scholars interpreted the statement of Allah the Exalted, ﴿And He found you lost (*dallan*) and guided you﴾ [Al-Duha: 7], on this basis, meaning *ghafilan* (heedless), according to one of the interpretations. This is confirmed by the statement of Allah the Exalted: ﴿You did not know what the Book was, nor faith﴾ [Al-Shura: 52]. [See vol. 20, p. 96, and vol. 16, p. 54.]

**Fifth**: Abdullah ibn Abd al-Hakam and Ashhab narrated from Malik, concerning the statement of Allah the Exalted, ﴿What is there after the truth except error?﴾, that he said: "Playing chess and backgammon is of error." Yunus narrated from Ibn Wahb that he was asked about a man who plays with his wife at home with fourteen (pieces), and Malik said: "I do not like it! It is not the way of the believers. Allah the Exalted says: ﴿What is there after the truth except error?﴾." Yunus also narrated from Ashhab that he said: "Malik was asked about playing chess, and he said: 'There is no good in it, it is nothing, it is of falsehood, and all play is of falsehood. A person of intellect should be restrained by his beard and his gray hair from falsehood.'" Al-Zuhri, when asked about chess, said: "It is of falsehood, and I do not like it."

**Sixth**: The scholars differed on the permissibility of playing chess and other games when it is not for gambling. The summary of the position of Malik and the majority of jurists regarding chess is that whoever does not gamble with it and plays with his family in his house, discreetly, once a month or a year, without being observed or known to be doing so, is pardoned and it is not forbidden to him nor disliked for him. But if he persists in it (*takhala'a*, indulged excessively and constantly, day and night) and becomes known for it, his integrity (*muruwwah*) and uprightness (*adalah*) fall away and his testimony is rejected.

As for al-Shafi'i, in the view of his companions the testimony of one who plays backgammon or chess is not invalidated, provided he is upright in all his conduct, and no foolishness, suspicion, or major sin appears from him, unless he plays it for gambling. If he plays it for gambling and is known for it, his uprightness falls away and he is considered foolish for consuming wealth through falsehood.

Abu Hanifa said: Playing chess, backgammon, the *arba'ata 'ashara* (the fourteen game), and all frivolity is disliked. If no major sin appears from the one who plays them and his good qualities outweigh his bad ones, his testimony is accepted according to them.

Ibn al-Arabi said: "The Shafi'is said that chess differs from backgammon, because it requires exertion of understanding and the use of natural talent. Backgammon is gambling, a game of chance (*gharar*), where one does not know what will come out for him, like seeking decision by arrows (*al-istiqsam bil-azlam*)."

**Seventh**: Our scholars said: "Backgammon is pieces filled with wood of *al-baqs* (a type of tree) and ivory, and likewise chess, for it is its brother, nourished with its milk." Backgammon is what is known as *al-batil* (the drum), and it is known as *al-ka'ab* (the dice bones), and it was known in the Jahiliyya also as *al-arun*, and also known as *nard shir*. [In manuscripts B, Ua, H, and Ya: "*al-tabl*" (the drum). In manuscript B: "*al-Arz*": we did not find in the books of chess or the dictionaries anything that resolves the matter.]

In the Sahih of Muslim, from Sulayman ibn Buraydah, from his father, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "Whoever plays backgammon (*nard shir*) is as if he dipped his hand in the flesh and blood of a pig." Our scholars said: "The meaning of this is that he is like one who dips his hand in the flesh of a pig, preparing it to eat it, and this act with regard to pork is forbidden and not permitted." This is clarified by his statement (ﷺ): "Whoever plays backgammon has disobeyed Allah and His Messenger." It was narrated by Malik and others from the hadith of Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, and it is a sound hadith. It forbids playing backgammon absolutely, and likewise chess. It did not exclude any time from any time nor any condition from any condition, and it informed that the doer of this is disobedient to Allah and His Messenger. However, it is possible that what is meant by playing backgammon that is forbidden is when it is for gambling, because of what is narrated of the permissibility of playing chess from the Followers (*tabi'un*) when not gambling. But it is understood in its generality, gambling and non-gambling, and that is more appropriate and more cautious, Allah willing.

Abu Abdullah al-Halimi said in his book *Minhaj al-Din*: "Among what has come concerning chess is a hadith narrated about it, just as it is narrated about backgammon, that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) said: 'Whoever plays chess has disobeyed Allah and His Messenger.'"

It is narrated from Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, that he passed by a gathering of the Banu Tamim who were playing chess, so he stopped over them and said: "Surely, by Allah, you were not created for this! By Allah, if it were not that it would become a sunnah, I would strike your faces with it."

Also from him, may Allah be pleased with him, that he passed by a people playing chess and said: "What are these images to which you are devoted? For one of you to touch a live coal until it is extinguished is better than to touch them."

Ibn Umar was asked about chess and said: "It is worse than backgammon." Abu Musa al-Ash'ari said: "No one plays chess except a sinner." Abu Ja'far was asked about chess and said: "Leave us from this Magianism."

In a long hadith from the Prophet (ﷺ): "Whoever plays backgammon, chess, *al-jawz* (nuts), and *al-ka'ab* (dice), Allah abhors him, and whoever sits with one who plays backgammon and chess to look at them, all his good deeds are erased from him and he becomes one whom Allah abhors."

All these reports indicate the prohibition of playing them without gambling, and Allah knows best. We have mentioned in *Surat al-Ma'ida* the explanation of their prohibition [See vol. 6, p. 291], and that they are like wine in prohibition due to their association with it, and Allah knows best.

Ibn al-Arabi said in his *Qabas*: "Al-Shafi'i permitted it, and the situation of some reached the point of saying: 'It is recommended,' so much so that they made it in the madrasa, and when the student became tired of reading, he played it in the mosque. They attributed to a group of the Companions and the Followers that they played it, but that never happened! By Allah, no pious person ever touched it. They say it sharpens the mind, but observation refutes them: no man with a mind ever excelled in it. I heard Imam Abu al-Fadl Ata al-Maqdisi say in the Al-Aqsa Mosque during a debate: 'It teaches warfare.' Al-Turtushi said to him: 'Rather, it corrupts the management of war, because the goal of war is the king and assassinating him, and in chess you say: *Shah iyyak* (the king, keep him away from my path),' so the attendees laughed."

At times Malik was strict about it and forbade it and said about it: ﴿What is there after the truth except error?﴾. At other times he was lenient about a little of it and the lesser of it. The first position is more correct, and Allah knows best.

If someone says: It was narrated from Umar ibn al-Khattab, may Allah be pleased with him, that he was asked about chess and said: "And what is chess?" It was said to him: "A woman had a son who was a king, and he was struck in a war away from his companions. She said: 'How can this be? Show it to me clearly.' So chess was made for her, and when she saw it she was consoled by it." They described chess to Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, and he said: "There is no harm in what is of the instruments of war."

It is said to him: This has no proof in it, because he did not say "there is no harm in chess," but said "there is no harm in what is of the instruments of war." He said this because it was confused for him that playing chess is among what is used to know the causes of war. When this was said to him and his knowledge did not encompass it, he said: "There is no harm in what is of the instruments of war. If it is as you say, then there is no harm in it." Likewise, what is narrated from the Companions that they did not forbid it is to be understood as their thinking that it is not used for amusement, but is intended as a means to knowledge of fighting and strategy in it, or because the connected report did not reach them.

Al-Halimi said: "When the report is sound, no one has any argument against it, and the proof is against everyone."

**Eighth**: Ibn Wahb narrated with his chain that Abdullah ibn Umar passed by boys playing with *al-kuja*, which are holes with pebbles in them that they play with, and he said: Ibn Umar filled them in and forbade them from them. Al-Harawi mentioned in the chapter of (*al-kaf* with *al-jim*), in the hadith of Ibn Abbas: "In everything there is gambling, even in the children's play with *al-kujja*." Ibn al-A'rabi said: "It is that the child takes a rag and rolls it as if it were a ball, then they gamble with it." And *kajja*, when he plays with the *kujja*.

ﷺ

﴿Then how are you turned away?﴾ That is, how do you turn your minds to worshipping what does not provide sustenance, nor give life, nor cause death?

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 10, verse 33:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Thus has the word of your Lord come true﴾, meaning His judgment, His decree, and His prior knowledge.

(Against those who defied) meaning they departed from obedience, disbelieved, and denied.

(That they will not believe) meaning they will not affirm. In this is the most conclusive proof against the Qadariyya (those who deny divine predestination). Nafi' and Ibn 'Amir recited here and at its end, "Thus have the words of your Lord come true," and in Surat Ghafir with the plural in all three places. The rest recited it in the singular. "Anna" (that) is in the accusative position, meaning "because they" or "for they." Al-Zajjaj said: It may also be in the nominative position as a substitution (badal) for "kalimat." Al-Farra' said: "Innahum" with a kasra is permissible as a fresh sentence (isti'naf).

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 10, verse 34:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: Is there any of your associates (shuraka'ikum) who originates creation and then repeats it?﴾ That is, your gods and objects of worship.

(Who originates creation and then repeats it.) That is, say to them, O Muhammad, this in the manner of rebuke and affirmation. If they answer you, well; otherwise, ﴿Say: It is Allah who originates creation and then repeats it.﴾ No one other than Him does that.

(So how are you turned away?) That is, how are you turned around and diverted from the truth to falsehood?

**Al-Qurtubi's commentary (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 10, verse 35:**

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Say: Is there any of your associates who guides to the truth?﴾ It is said: "hadahu lil-tariq" and "hadahu ila al-tariq" have the same meaning (he guided him to the way). This has already been discussed [[See vol. 1, p. 160.]]. That is, "Is there any of your associates who guides to the religion of Islam?" If they say, "No, and there must be," then say to them: "Allah guides to the truth." Then say to them, rebuking and affirming: ﴿Is He who guides to the truth more worthy to be followed, or he who does not guide unless he is guided?﴾

(*Afaman yahdi*): that is, guides, gives direction.

(*Ila al-haqq*): and He is Allah, glorified and exalted.

(*Ahaqqu an yuttaba'a amman la yahiddi illa an yuhda*): He means the idols, which guide no one, and do not walk unless they are carried, and do not move from their place unless they are moved. The poet said [[He is Tarafah, as in Lisan al-Arab.]]:

"For the youth there is an intellect by which he lives,
wherever his foot guides his leg."

It is also said that the intended meaning is the leaders and the misleaders, who do not guide themselves to any guidance unless they are guided.

Regarding "yahdi" there are six readings. **The first:** the people of Madina, except Warsh, read "yahaddi" with a fatha on the ya', a sukun on the ha', and a shadda on the dal. Thus in their recitation they combined two sakin letters, as they did in His saying "la ta'uddu" [[See vol. 6, p. 7.]] and in His saying "yakhissimun." Al-Nahhas said: "No one can pronounce the combination of two sakin letters." Muhammad ibn Yazid said: "Whoever attempts such a thing must move the letter with a light vowel toward kasra," and Sibawayh calls this *ikhtilas al-haraka* (the rapid, reduced vowel).

**The second:** Abu 'Amr and Qalun, in one transmission, read it between fatha and sukun, in accordance with their method of *ikhfa'* (partial vocalization) and *ikhtilas*.

**The third:** Ibn 'Amir, Ibn Kathir, Warsh, and Ibn Muhaysin read "yahaddi" with a fatha on the ya' and the ha', and a shadda on the dal. Al-Nahhas said: "This reading is clear in Arabic, and its origin is *yahtadi*, where the ta' was assimilated into the dal and its vowel was transferred to the ha'."

**The fourth:** Hafs, Ya'qub, and al-A'mash, from Abu Bakr, read like Ibn Kathir's reading, except that they put a kasra on the ha'. They said: "Because when the jazm (sukun) must be moved, it is moved to kasra." Abu Hatim said: "This is the dialect of the lower Mudar."

**The fifth:** Abu Bakr, from 'Asim, read "yihaddi" with a kasra on the ya' and the ha', and a shadda on the dal, all to follow the kasra, as was previously mentioned in al-Baqarah concerning "yakhtafu" [[See vol. 1, p. 221.]] (2:20). It is also said that this is the dialect of those who read "nasta'in" [[See vol. 1, p. 641.]] and "lan tamassana al-nar" and similar forms. Sibawayh does not permit "yihaddi," but he permits "tihaddi," "nihaddi," and "ihaddi," saying: "Because the kasra on the ya' is heavy."

**The sixth:** Hamza, al-Kisa'i, Khalaf, Yahya ibn Wththáb, and al-A'mash read "yahdi" with a fatha on the ya', a sukun on the ha', and a light dal (no shadda), from *hada, yahdi*. Al-Nahhas said: "This reading has two possible grammatical explanations in Arabic, though it is remote. One of the two is that al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' said: 'yahdi' means 'yahtadi' (is guided). Abu al-'Abbas said: 'This is not known. Rather, the meaning is: *amman la yahdi ghayrahu* (who does not guide others), and the sentence is complete. Then He said: *illa an yuhda* (unless he is guided), which begins a new statement from the first, meaning: but he needs to be guided. So it is a disjunctive exception (*istithna' munqati'*), as you say: 'So-and-so does not make anyone hear except that he himself is made to hear,' meaning: but he needs to be made to hear.'"

Abu Ishaq said: "*Fa-ma lakum*" is a complete sentence, and the meaning is: "What, then, is the matter with you in worshipping idols?" Then it was said to them: ﴿How do you judge?﴾ That is, for yourselves, and you pass judgment with this clear falsehood, worshipping gods that cannot avail themselves of anything, unless they are acted upon, while Allah does what He wills, and you abandon His worship. Therefore the position of *kayfa* (how) is in the accusative, governed by *tahkumun* (you judge).

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And most of them follow nothing but conjecture﴾. He means their leaders, that is, they follow only guesswork and conjecture regarding their being gods and their being intercessors, and they have no proof with them. As for their followers, they follow them by blind imitation (taqlid).

﴿Indeed, conjecture avails nothing against the truth﴾, that is, against the punishment of Allah, for the Truth is Allah. It has also been said that "the truth" here means certainty, i.e., conjecture is not like certainty. This verse is evidence that conjecture is not sufficient in matters of belief ('aqa'id).

﴿Indeed, Allah is Knowing of what they do﴾, of disbelief and denial. It is phrased as a threat.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 10, verse 37:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And this Qur'an could not have been produced by other than Allah﴾. "An" (that) together with "yuftara" (it be fabricated) forms a verbal noun (masdar), and the meaning is: "This Qur'an was not a fabrication," just as you say: "So-and-so loves that he rides," meaning, "he loves riding." This was said by al-Kisa'i. Al-Farra' said: the meaning is "It is not fitting for this Qur'an that it be fabricated," like His saying: ﴿It is not for a prophet to embezzle﴾ [Al 'Imran: 161] and ﴿It is not for the believers to go forth all together﴾ [al-Tawbah: 122]. It was also said that "an" carries the meaning of the lam (in order that), its implied sense being: "This Qur'an was not such that it should be fabricated." It was also said that it carries the meaning of "la" (not), i.e., "it is not fabricated." It was also said that the meaning is: it was not possible for anyone to bring the like of this Qur'an from other than Allah and then attribute it to Allah, the Exalted, because of its inimitability, owing to its description (wasf), its meanings, and its composition.

(But a confirmation of what is between its hands) Al-Kisa'i, al-Farra' and Muhammad ibn Sa'dan said: the implied reading is "but it was a confirmation" (taṣdīq), and in their view the nominative is also permissible, meaning: "but it is a confirmation." "What is between its hands" means: from the Torah, the Gospel and other books, for they had given glad tidings of it, so it came confirming them in that glad tidings, and in calling to monotheism and belief in the Resurrection. It was also said that the meaning is: "but a confirmation of the Prophet who is between the hands of the Qur'an," and he is Muhammad (ﷺ), because they had witnessed him before they heard the Qur'an from him.

(And an elaboration of the Book) in the accusative and nominative, on the two readings mentioned for "taṣdīq." "Tafsil" means explanation, i.e., it explains what is in the earlier Books of Allah. "Al-Kitab" is a generic noun. It was also said that by "the elaboration of the Book" he meant the rulings that are made clear in the Qur'an.

(there is no doubt in it) The pronoun "hu" refers to the Qur'an, i.e., there is no doubt in it, that is, regarding its descent from Allah, the Exalted.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 10, verse 38:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Or do they say, "He has invented it"?﴾ Am (أم) here is in the place of the interrogative alif, because it is joined to what precedes it. It is also said: it is the disjunctive am (أمِ المنقطعة), which is estimated to mean "bal" (rather) together with the hamza, as in His saying, may He be exalted: "Alif-Lam-Mim. The revelation of the Book, in which there is no doubt, is from the Lord of the worlds" [see vol. 14, p. ...]. ﴿Or do they say, "He has invented it"?﴾ [As-Sajdah: 3, 2, 1], meaning: "Rather, do they say, 'He has invented it'?" Abu 'Ubaydah said: am here means waw (and), its sense being: "And they say, 'He has invented it.'" It is also said: the mim is a connecting particle, and the estimate is: "Do they say, 'He has invented it'?" That is, Muhammad invented the Qur'an from his own self. So it is an interrogative whose meaning is rebuke.

﴿Say: Then bring a surah like it.﴾ The meaning of the statement is argument, for the previous verse indicated that the Qur'an is from Allah, since it confirms what lies before it of the Books and agrees with them, without Muhammad, peace be upon him, having learned from anyone. This verse is a challenge that they bring a surah like it if it is fabricated. The discussion of the inimitability (i'jaz) of the Qur'an, and that it is inimitable, has already passed in the introduction of the book [see vol. 1, p. 69], and praise be to Allah.

Al-Qurtubi's commentary on Surah 10, verse 39:

God's words: ﴿Nay, they denied that which they did not encompass in knowledge﴾, meaning: they denied the Qur'an while they were ignorant of its meanings and its tafsir (exegesis). It is incumbent upon them to acquire that knowledge by asking, and this indicates that one must look into ta'wil (the ultimate meaning or realization of a statement). His words, ﴿and its ta'wil has not yet come to them﴾, mean: the true outcome of denial, namely the descent of punishment upon them, has not yet come to them. Or, they denied what the Qur'an contains concerning the Resurrection, Paradise and Hellfire, and its ta'wil had not yet come to them, i.e., the reality of what they were promised in the Book. This was said by al-Dahhak.

It was said to al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl: "Do you find in the Qur'an, 'Whoever is ignorant of something becomes its enemy'?" He said: "Yes, in two places: ﴿Nay, they denied that which they did not encompass in knowledge﴾, and His saying: ﴿And since they have not been guided by it, they will say, 'This is an ancient falsehood'﴾ [Al-Ahqaf: 11]." [See vol. 16, p. 189 onward.]

God's words: ﴿Thus did those before them deny﴾, meaning the earlier nations, i.e., this was their way. The kaf (ك) in this phrase is in a position of nasb (accusative).

﴿So see how was the end of the wrongdoers﴾, i.e., their being seized with destruction and punishment.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 10, verse 40:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And among them are those who believe in it﴾. It was said: the intended people are the people of Makkah, meaning: among them are those who will believe in it in the future, even if their denial lasts long, because of His, exalted is He, prior knowledge concerning them that they are among the blessed. The word "man" (من) is in the nominative case as the subject (mubtada'), and the predicate is in the prepositional phrase (al-majrur). [[In manuscript ʿayn: "in the prepositional phrase (al-jar wa-al-majrur)."]] And likewise.

(And among them are those who do not believe in it.) The meaning: among them are those who persist in their disbelief until they die, such as Abu Talib, Abu Lahab, and their like. It was also said: the intended people are the People of the Book. It was also said: it is general to all disbelievers, and this is the sound view. It was also said that the pronoun in "bihi" (in it) refers to Muhammad ﷺ, so Allah, glorified is He, informed that He only delayed the punishment because among them are those who will believe.

(And your Lord knows best the corrupters.) That is, those who persist in their disbelief, and this is a warning to them.

"His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And if they deny you, then say: 'For me is my work, and for you is your work.'﴾ [It] is in the nominative case as the subject of a nominal sentence (mubtada'), and the meaning is: for me is the reward of my work in conveying (the message), in warning, and in obedience to Allah, exalted is He.

(And for you is your work), i.e. its recompense of polytheism.

(You are free of what I do, and I am free of what you do) is similar to it, i.e. no one is held to account for another's sin. This verse is abrogated (mansukh) by the verse of the sword (ayat al-sayf), according to the saying of Mujahid, al-Kalbi, Muqatil and Ibn Zayd."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 10, verses 42–43:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And among them are those who listen to you﴾. He means by their outward forms, while their hearts do not comprehend anything of the truth that he (the Prophet) says or of the Qur'an that he recites. For this reason He said: (Can you make the deaf hear, even though they do not use their intellect?), that is, you cannot make them hear. Its outward form is a question, but its meaning is negation. He made them like the deaf because of the sealing upon their hearts and the stamping upon them, that is, you are not able to guide one whom Allah has made deaf to hearing the guidance. Likewise the meaning in: "And among them are those who look at you. Can you guide the blind, even though they do not see?" Allah, exalted is He, informed that no one believes except by His enabling grace and His guidance. This and what is similar to it refutes the Qadariyya in their saying, as has been mentioned in more than one place. He said "yastami'un" (listen) according to the meaning of "man" (those), and "yanzuru" (look) according to the wording. The purpose is to console the Prophet ﷺ, that is, just as you cannot make hear the one whom Allah has deprived of hearing, nor can you create sight for the blind by which he may be guided, so likewise you cannot grant these people faith, and Allah has decreed upon them that they will not believe. The meaning of "yanzuru ilayka" (looks at you) is that he keeps gazing at you, as He said: ﴿They look at you, their eyes rolling like one who faints from death﴾ [al-Ahzab: 19] [[see vol. 14, p. ]]. It has been said: it was revealed concerning the mockers, and Allah knows best.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 10, verses 42–43:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And among them are those who listen to you﴾. He means by their outward forms, while their hearts do not comprehend anything of the truth that he (the Prophet) says or of the Qur'an that he recites.
