Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 10, verse 44:

When He mentioned the people of wretchedness, He mentioned that He did not wrong them, and that the decree of wretchedness upon them, and the stripping away of the hearing of the heart and its sight, is not an injustice from Him, because He disposes of His dominion as He wills, and He is just in all of His actions. "But it is people themselves who wrong themselves" by disbelief, disobedience, and opposing the command of their Creator. Hamzah and al-Kisa'i recited "wa-lakin" with the (ل) "lakin" lightened (ـكن مخففا) and "al-nas" in the nominative (رفعا). Al-Nahhas said: A group of grammarians, among them al-Farra', claimed that when the Arabs say "wa-lakinna" with the waw, they prefer the doubling (tashdid), and when they drop the waw, they prefer lightening (takhfif). He gave the reason for this, saying: Because when it is without a waw, it resembles "bal" (rather), so they lightened it so that what follows it would be like what follows "bal." And when they bring the waw, it differs from "bal," so they doubled it and put the accusative after it, because it is "inna" to which a lam and a kaf have been added and it has been made a single particle. And he recited:

But I, from my love for her, am indeed a lovesick one (wa-lakinnani min hubbiha la-'amid)

He brought the lam because it is "inna."

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 10, verse 45:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And [mention] the Day He will gather them, [and it will be] as if they had not remained [in the world] except an hour of the day﴾. It means: as if they had not remained in their graves. (The phrase "as if" here) is kaannahum with the letters lightened, i.e., as if they had not remained in their graves.

(Except an hour of the day) means: about the length of an hour. The meaning is that they will consider the length of their stay in the graves to be short, because of the terror of what they see of the resurrection. Its evidence is their saying: ﴿We remained a day or part of a day﴾ [Al-Kahf: 19]. It was also said: the duration of their stay in the world seemed short to them because of the terror of what they faced, not the duration of their being in the grave. Ibn 'Abbas said: they will see that the length of their lives, compared to eternity, is like an hour.

(They will recognize one another among themselves) is in a place of accusative as a circumstantial clause (hal) from the hu and mim in "yahshuruhum." It may also be an independent (munqati') clause, as if he said: so they recognize one another. Al-Kalbi said: some of them will recognize others as they recognized them in the world when they come out of their graves. This recognition is a recognition of rebuke and exposure: one of them says to another, "You misled me, you seduced me, and you drove me to disbelief," not a recognition of compassion, tenderness, or affection. Then the recognition will cease when they witness the terrors of the Day of Resurrection, as He said: ﴿And no intimate friend will ask after an intimate friend﴾ [Al-Ma'arij: 10]. It was also said: the recognition of rebuke remains, and this is the sound view, because of His saying: "And if only you could see when the wrongdoers are made to stand before their Lord..." up to His saying ﴿and We will put shackles upon the necks of those who disbelieved﴾ [Saba': 31-33], and His saying: ﴿Every time a nation enters, it curses its sister﴾ [Al-A'raf: 38], and the verse, and His saying: ﴿Our Lord, indeed we obeyed our leaders and our elders﴾ [Al-Ahzab: 67], and so on. As for His saying: "And no intimate friend will ask after an intimate friend," and His saying: ﴿So when the Horn is blown, there will be no relationships among them﴾ [Al-Mu'minun: 101], its meaning is that he will not ask him out of mercy or compassion, and Allah knows best. It was also said: the Resurrection has stages. It was also said: the meaning of "yatarafun" is "yatasa'alun" (they question one another), i.e., they ask one another how long they remained, as He said: ﴿And some of them will turn to others, questioning one another﴾ [Al-Saffat: 27]. This is good. Al-Dahhak said: that is the recognition of the affection of the believers, and the disbelievers have no affection toward them, as He said: "there will be no relationships among them." The first view is more apparent, and Allah knows best.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those who denied the meeting with Allah have certainly lost﴾, i.e., by being presented before Allah. It was then said: this may be a report from Allah, mighty and majestic is He, after He indicated the resurrection and the raising, meaning they lost the reward of Paradise. It was also said: they lost at the time of meeting Allah, because loss is only in that state in which there is no hope of retraction and repentance no longer benefits. Al-Nahhas said: the meaning may also be that they will recognize one another, saying this. "And they were not guided" means, according to the knowledge of Allah.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 10, verse 46:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Whether We show you﴾ is a conditional clause (shart).

(Some of) what We promise them: that is, some of the manifestation of your religion during your lifetime. The commentators said: the part of what He promised them was the killing of those who were killed and the capture of those who were taken captive at Badr.

(Or We take you in death) is conjoined (ma'tuf) to "We show you," meaning: We take you in death before that.

(Then to Us is their return) is the response (jawab) to "whether" (imma). The intended meaning is: if We do not take vengeance upon them quickly, We will take vengeance upon them later.

(Then Allah is Witness) means: a Witness who needs no witness.

(Over what they do) of fighting against you and denying you. If it were said, "Then Allah is Witness" with the meaning of "there" (hunak), it would be permissible.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 10, verse 47:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And for every nation there is a messenger. So when their messenger comes, judgment will be made between them with justice﴾. The meaning is: for every nation there is a messenger as a witness over them, and when their messenger comes on the Day of Resurrection, judgment will be made between them. Like His saying: ﴿So how will it be when We bring from every nation a witness﴾ [An-Nisa: 41].[[See vol. 5, p. 197.]] Ibn 'Abbas said: The disbelievers will deny, on the Day of Reckoning, the coming of the messengers to them. The messenger will then be brought and will say: "I have indeed conveyed the message to you." Then judgment of punishment will be passed upon them. Its evidence is His saying: ﴿and the Messenger will be a witness over you﴾.[[See vol. 2, p. 153.]] It is also possible that the meaning is that they are not punished in this world until a messenger is sent to them; whoever believes succeeds and is saved, and whoever does not believe perishes and is punished. Its evidence is His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We would not punish until We have sent a messenger﴾ [Al-Isra: 15].[[See vol. 10, p. 230 onward.]] Al-qist (القِسْط) means justice.

(And they will not be wronged) i.e., they will not be punished without sin, nor will they be held accountable without proof.

The disbelievers of Makkah are meant here, because of their excessive denial and their hasty demand for the punishment, meaning: when is the punishment, or when is the Resurrection that Muhammad promises us? It was also said that the verse is general, referring to every nation that denied its messenger.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 10, verse 49:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: I possess not for myself any harm or benefit﴾. When they urged the Prophet ﷺ to hasten the punishment, Allah said to him: Say to them, O Muhammad, "I possess not for myself any harm or benefit," meaning that this is not in my power nor in the power of anyone else.

(Except what Allah wills) that I should possess it and have power over it. So how could I have power to possess what you are hastening? Therefore do not hasten.

(For every nation there is a term) meaning that for their destruction and punishment there is a appointed time, known in His knowledge, glorified is He.

(When their term comes) meaning the time of the end of their term.

(Then they cannot delay it an hour, nor can they advance it) meaning that it is not possible for them to remain in this world for even an hour longer, nor to advance it and thus postpone it.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 10, verse 50:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Say: Have you considered, if His punishment should come upon you by night or by day?﴾ "By night" and "by day" are two adverbs of time (zarfan). This is a reply to their saying, "When is this promise?" and a rebuke of their opinions in hastening the punishment. That is, if the punishment comes upon you, what benefit will you gain from it, and faith will not benefit you at that time.

﴿What is it that the criminals seek to hasten?﴾ This is an interrogative whose meaning is to terrify and to magnify, that is, how great is that which they seek to hasten. It is like saying to someone who pursues a matter whose outcome is considered harmful: "What are you bringing upon yourself!" The pronoun in "minhu" (from it) is said to refer to the punishment, and it is said to refer to Allah, glorified and exalted. Al-Nahhas said: If you make the pronoun in "minhu" refer to the punishment, then for "madha" (what) you have two possible analyses. The first is that "ma" is in the nominative position as the subject (mubtada'), and "dha" means "alladhi" (which), serving as the predicate of "ma," with the returning pronoun omitted; the second estimation is that "madha" is a single word in the nominative position as the subject, and the predicate is in the sentence, as said by al-Zajjaj. If you make the pronoun in "minhu" refer to the name of Allah, the Exalted, then "ma" and "dha" are one thing, and it is in the accusative position governed by "yasta'jilu" (seek to hasten), and the meaning is: what thing do the criminals seek to hasten from Allah, Mighty and Majestic?

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 10, verse 51:

Allah's words: ﴿Is it then, when it has befallen you, that you believe in it now?﴾ There is an ellipsis in the speech, and the implied meaning is: "Do you feel secure that the punishment will descend upon you, and then it will be said to you when it has come down: 'Do you now believe in it?'" It was said: this is from the words of the angels, mocking them. And it was said: this is from the words of Allah, the Exalted. The interrogative alif (hamzat al-istifham) has entered upon "thumma" (then), and the meaning is affirmation and rebuke, and to indicate that the meaning of the second clause follows the first. It was also said: "thumma" here has the meaning of "thumma" with a fatha on the tha', so that it is an adverb of place, and the meaning is "there" (ahunālika), and this is the view of al-Tabari; in that case there is no meaning of interrogation in it. As for "al-An" (now), it was said: its origin is a verb built like "han" (it has come time), and the alif and lam are for transforming it into a noun. Al-Khalil said: it was built because of the meeting of two unvocalized letters (sakinayn), and the alif and lam are for definiteness and pointing to the time, and it is the boundary between the two periods of time.

(And you used to seek to hasten it) i.e., the punishment.

"Then it will be said to those who did wrong": that is, the keepers of Hell will say to them.

﴿Taste the punishment of eternity﴾: that is, the one that does not end.

﴿Are you being recompensed except for what you used to earn?﴾: that is, the recompense of your disbelief.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 10, verse 53:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿They ask you to inform them (wa-yastanbi'unaka)﴾, i.e., they ask you for information, O Muhammad, about the punishment and the establishment of the Hour (qiyam al-sa'ah).

(Ahaqqun) is a beginning (ibtida', the grammatical subject-initiating construction).

(Huwa) fills the place of the predicate (sadda masadda al-khabar), and this is the opinion of Sibawayh. It is also permissible for "huwa" to be the subject (mubtada') and "ahaqqun" its predicate (khabar).

(Qul ii) "ii" is a word of affirmation, confirmation and emphasis, meaning "yes" (na'am).

(Wa-rabbi) is an oath.

(Innahu la-haqqun) is its answer (jawabuhu), meaning: it is certainly something that exists, with no doubt about it.

(Wa-ma antum bi-mu'jizin) means: you will not escape from His punishment and His requital (fa'ita, "escaping" or "eluding").

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 10, verse 54:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And if every soul that had wronged had whatever is in the earth﴾, i.e., had associated partners with Allah and disbelieved.

(Whatever is in the earth) i.e., as possession.

(They would surely ransom themselves with it) i.e., from the punishment of Allah, meaning it would not be accepted from them, as He said: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve and die while they are disbelievers, never will be accepted from any of them the earth filled with gold even if he should offer it for ransom﴾ [Surah Al 'Imran: 91]. This has already been mentioned [see vol. 4, p. 131].

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And they will conceal the regret﴾, i.e., they will hide it, meaning their leaders, i.e., they will hide their regret from their followers.

(When they see the punishment) and this is before being burned by the Fire. When they fall into the Fire, the Fire diverts them from feigning, as evidenced by their saying: (Our Lord, our wretchedness overcame us) [see vol. 12, p. 153]. So it shows that they do not conceal what is in them. It has also been said that "asarru" means "they displayed," and the word is among the words with two opposite meanings (addad), and what supports this is that the Hereafter is not a place of steadfastness and patience. It has also been said: they found the pain of anguish in their hearts, because regret cannot be displayed. Kathir said:

"So I concealed the regret on the day the caller called / with the rapid camels of Ghadirah, the caller..."

Al-Mubarrad mentioned a third meaning regarding it: that by the regret, the "asirrah" (creases) of their faces appeared, which are the folds of the forehead, its singular being "sirar." And "nadamah" (regret) is grief over the occurrence of something or the loss of something, and its origin is adherence, from which comes "nadim" (companion), because he is attached to gatherings. And it is said: "Fulan nadim sadim." And "sadm" is persistence in a matter. And "nadima" and "tanadama" with something means he was concerned with it. Al-Jawhari said: "al-sadam" (with a fatha on the sad and the sukun on the dal, in the sense of a vowel-pattern) is regret and sorrow, and one says "sadima" (with kasra), meaning he became concerned and grieved, and a man is "nadim sadim," and "nadman sadman." It is said that it is an echo-formation (ittba'). "He has no concern and no sadm except that." It has also been said: "al-nadam" is an inversion of "al-daman," and "al-daman" is adherence, from which comes "Fulan mudmin al-khamr" (so-and-so is addicted to wine). And "al-dimn" is what gathers in a house and becomes matted of urine and dung, named so for its adherence. And "al-dimnah" is the rancor that clings to the chest, its plural being "dimanun." And their hearts have become "dimina" (with kasra), it is said: "Damintu 'ala fulan," meaning I harbored resentment against so-and-so.

(And it will be judged between them with justice) i.e., between the leaders and the followers, with fairness.

(And they will not be wronged).

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 10, verse 55:

(Alā) is a word of alerting the listener, added at the beginning of speech, meaning: "Pay attention to what I am telling you." (Inna lillāhi mā fī as-samāwāti wal-arḍ. Alā inna waʿda Allāhi ḥaqq), ﴿To Him belongs the dominion of the heavens and the earth﴾ [al-Hadid: 2]. So nothing prevents Him from carrying out what He has promised [[In ʿ: ḥukmuhu (His decree).]].

(But most of them do not know) that.

Qurtubi's commentary on Surah Yunus (10), verse 56:

He explained the meaning. And it has already been mentioned.

"O mankind" — he said, meaning the Quraysh.

(There has certainly come to you an admonition) — i.e., an exhortation.

(from your Lord) — meaning the Qur'an, which contains admonitions and wisdoms.

(and a healing for what is in the breasts) — i.e., from doubt, hypocrisy, dissension and discord.

(and guidance) — i.e., and right direction for whoever follows it.

(and a mercy) — i.e., a blessing.

(for the believers) — He specified them because they are the ones who benefit through faith. All of these are attributes of the Qur'an, and the conjunction (wa, "and") serves to emphasize the praise. The poet said:

"To the mighty king and the son of the lofty one... and the lion of the battalion in the crowd."

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 10, verse 58:**

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Say: "By the bounty of Allah and by His mercy"﴾. Abu Sa'id al-Khudri and Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, said: "The bounty of Allah is the Qur'an, and His mercy is Islam." Also from them both: "The bounty of Allah is the Qur'an, and His mercy is that He made you among its people." From al-Hasan, al-Dahhak, Mujahid and Qatadah: "The bounty of Allah is faith (iman), and His mercy is the Qur'an," the reverse of the first view. It has also been said: "other than this."

(﴿So let them rejoice in that﴾) refers to the bounty and the mercy. The Arabs use "bi-dhalika" (in that) for the singular, the dual and the plural. It is narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he recited "fa-bi-dhalika fa-l-tafrahu" with the letter ta', and this is the recitation (qira'ah) of Yazid ibn al-Qa'qa', Ya'qub and others. In the hadith there is also (li-ta'khudhu masaffakum), "that you may take your ranks." Joy (farah) is a pleasure in the heart at attaining what is loved. Joy has been condemned in several places, such as His saying: ﴿Do not rejoice; indeed Allah does not love the rejoicers﴾ [Al-Qasas: 76], and His saying: ﴿Indeed, he is exultant and boastful﴾ [Hud: 10]. However, it is unrestricted there. When joy is restricted, it is not blameworthy, according to His saying: ﴿Rejoicing in what Allah has given them of His bounty﴾ [Al 'Imran: 170]. Here, the Blessed and Exalted said: "fa-bi-dhalika fa-l-yafrahu," meaning: "let them rejoice in the Qur'an and Islam," so it is restricted. Harun said: "In the reading of Ubayy it is 'fa-bi-dhalika fa-fraḥu' (rejoice)." Al-Nahhas said: "The usual form of the imperative is with the lam, so that it has a jussive particle, just as the prohibition has a particle. However, they omit the lam from the imperative addressed to the second person, relying on the address itself. Sometimes they keep it in its original form, as in 'fa-bi-dhalika fa-l-tafrahu'."

(﴿It is better than what they accumulate﴾) means in this world. The common reading is with the ya' in both verbs ("fa-l-yafrahu" and "yajma'un"). It is narrated from Ibn 'Amir that he read "fa-l-yafrahu" with the ya' and "tajma'un" with the ta', as an address to the disbelievers. It is narrated from al-Hasan that he read with the ta' in the first verb and with the ya' in "yajma'un," the reverse of this. Aban narrated from Anas that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Whoever Allah has guided to Islam, and taught the Qur'an, and then complains of poverty, Allah will write poverty between his eyes until the day he meets Him." Then he recited: "Say: 'By the bounty of Allah and by His mercy, so let them rejoice in that; it is better than what they accumulate.'"

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 10, verse 59:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Say: Have you considered what God has sent down to you of provision, and you have made some of it unlawful and some lawful?﴾ In this there are two issues.

The first: His saying, ﴿Say: Have you considered?﴾ addresses the disbelievers of Makkah.

(What God has sent down to you of provision) "Ma" is in the accusative position governed by "ara'aytum" (have you considered). Al-Zajjaj said: it is in the accusative position governed by "anzala" (sent down). "Anzala" here means "khalaqa" (created), as He said: ﴿And He sent down for you eight pairs of livestock﴾ [al-Zumar: 6] (see vol. 15, p. 234), and ﴿And We sent down iron, wherein is great might﴾ [al-Hadid: 25] (see vol. 17, p. 260). Thus it is permissible to express creation by "sending down," because the provision that is on the earth is only by what descends from the sky, namely the rain.

(And you have made some of it unlawful and some lawful) Mujahid said: it refers to what they ruled to be forbidden, such as the bahirah, the sa'ibah, the wasilah and the ham (see vol. 6, p. 335). Al-Dahhak said: it refers to the saying of God, may He be exalted: ﴿And they assign to God a share of what He has created of the tilth and the livestock﴾ (see vol. 7, p. 89) [al-An'am: 136].

(Say: Has God permitted you?) That is, to make lawful and unlawful.

(Or do you invent against God?) "Am" here means "bal" (rather).

(You invent) is their saying that God commanded us to do so.

The second: Whoever denies analogy (qiyas) has used this verse as evidence, but this is far-fetched, for analogy is an indication from God, may He be exalted, so that making lawful and making unlawful come from God, may He be exalted, when there is an indication which God has established for the ruling. If someone disagrees that analogy is an indication from God, may He be exalted, then he has departed from this purpose and turned to something else.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 10, verse 60:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And what will be the thought of those who invent lies against Allah on the Day of Resurrection?﴾ "Yawm" (the Day) is in the accusative as an adverb of time (zarf), or it is governed by "al-zann" (thought/supposition), as in the construction "ma zannuka Zaydan" (what do you think of Zayd). The meaning is: Do they suppose that Allah will not hold them accountable for it?

(Indeed, Allah is full of bounty toward mankind) meaning, in deferring (their punishment) and granting them respite. It was also said: it refers to the people of Makkah when He placed them in a secure sanctuary (haram).

(But most of them) meaning, the disbelievers.

(do not give thanks) to Allah for His blessings, nor for His deferring the punishment from them. It was also said: "do not give thanks" means they do not affirm the oneness of Allah (tawhid).

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 10, verse 61:

His words, may He be exalted: ﴿And you are not engaged in any matter﴾ "Ma" (ما) here is for negation, meaning: you are not in any matter, that is, of worship or anything else, except that the Lord is watching you. Al-sha'n (الشأن) means the affair and the matter, and its plural is shu'un (شئون). Al-Akhfash said: the Arabs say, "ma sha'anta sha'anahu," meaning, "you did not do his deed."

(﴿And you do not recite from it any Qur'an﴾) Al-Farra' and al-Zajjaj said: the pronoun in "minhu" (منه) refers to the matter, meaning: a matter arises, so the Qur'an is recited concerning it, so that its ruling is known, or a Qur'an is revealed concerning it and then recited. Al-Tabari said: "minhu" means from the Book of Allah, the Exalted. "Min Qur'an" (from Qur'an) is repeated for emphasis, like His words: ﴿Indeed, I am Allah﴾ [al-Qasas: 30].[[See vol. 13, p. 283.]]

(﴿Nor do you do any deed﴾) He addresses the Prophet ﷺ and the community. His words "And you are not engaged in any matter" are addressed to him, while what is meant is him and his community; the Messenger may be addressed while what is meant is him and his followers. It is also said that what is meant is the disbelievers of Quraysh.

(﴿Except that We are witnesses over you﴾) meaning, We know it. Its parallel is His words: ﴿There is no secret conference of three but that He is their fourth﴾ [al-Mujadila: 4]. (﴿When you are involved in it﴾) meaning, you take up with it; the pronoun refers to the deed. It is said: "Fulan afada fi al-hadith wa al-'amal" (فلان أفاض في الحديث والعمل) when he plunges into it. Al-Ra'i said:

"Then they poured forth, after their silence, with a cud-chewing from Dhi al-Abatih, when they had grazed the hameel."

Ibn 'Abbas: "tufidun fihi" (تفيضون فيه) means you do it. Al-Akhfash: you speak. Ibn Zayd: you plunge in. Ibn Kaysan: you spread the saying. Al-Dahhak said: the pronoun refers to the Qur'an, meaning: when you spread falsehood concerning the Qur'an.

(﴿And not absent from your Lord﴾) Ibn 'Abbas said: it is hidden. Abu Rawq said: it is far off. Ibn Kaysan said: it goes away. Al-Kisa'i read "ya'zub" (يعزب) with a kasra on the zay wherever it occurs, while the others read it with a damma; both are eloquent dialects, like "ya'rish" and "ya'rush" (يعرش ويعرش).

(﴿Of the weight of﴾) "Min" (من) is superfluous, meaning: and the weight of (مثقال) ﴿an atom's﴾ (ذرة) is not absent from your Lord, that is, the weight of an atom, which is a small red ant, and it has been mentioned earlier in (al-Nisa').[[See vol. 5, p. 195.]]

(﴿in the earth or in the heaven, nor anything smaller than that or greater﴾) is conjoined to the wording "mithqal," and if you wish, to "dharra." Ya'qub and Hamza read the ra' in both with a damma, conjoining them to the position of "mithqal," because "min" is superfluous for emphasis. Al-Zajjaj said: the nominative is also permissible as an inchoative, and its predicate is (﴿except that it is in a clear Record﴾), meaning the Preserved Tablet together with Allah's knowledge of it. Al-Jurjani said: "illa" (إلا) here carries the meaning of the conjunctive waw (واو النسق), meaning "and it is in a clear Record," like His words: ﴿Indeed, the messengers do not fear in My presence, except one who wrongs﴾ [al-Naml: 10-11], meaning "and one who wrongs." And His words: ﴿so that people will have no argument against you, except those of them who do wrong﴾ [al-Baqarah: 150], meaning "and those of them who did wrong." So "illa" is in the sense of the conjunctive waw, and a predicate is implied after it, as in His words: ﴿And say, "Hittah"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 58], meaning "it is Hittah." And His words: ﴿And do not say, "Three"﴾ [al-Nisa': 171], meaning "they are three." A parallel to what we are discussing is: ﴿And not a leaf falls but He knows it, nor a grain within the darknesses of the earth, nor anything moist or dry but that it is in a clear Record﴾ [al-An'am: 59], meaning "and it is in a clear Record."

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Qur'an) on Surah 10 (Yunus), verse 62:**

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿Unquestionably, the friends of Allah—there is no fear for them~~~~ (i.e., in the Hereafter), "nor shall they grieve," (i.e., over the loss of worldly things). It was also said: "There is no fear for them, nor shall they grieve" means: those whom Allah, Exalted is He, takes as His friend, whose protection and safeguarding He undertakes, and with whom He is pleased, so they will not fear on the Day of Resurrection nor will they grieve. Allah, Exalted is He, said: "Indeed, those for whom the good reward has preceded from Us—those will be kept far away from it" (i.e., from Hell), "[who will be] kept far away" [[see vol. 11, p. 345]] [al-Anbiya' 101–103], up to His words: ﴿The greatest terror will not grieve them﴾.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr narrated that the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) was asked: "Who are the friends of Allah?" He said: "Those who, by seeing them, Allah is remembered."

Umar ibn al-Khattab said regarding this verse: I heard the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) say: "Indeed, among the servants of Allah are servants who are neither prophets nor martyrs, yet the prophets and martyrs will envy them on the Day of Resurrection because of their standing with Allah, Exalted is He." It was said: "O Messenger of Allah, tell us who they are and what their deeds are, so that we may love them." He said: "They are a people who loved one another for the sake of Allah, not through kinship between them nor through wealth they exchange. By Allah, their faces are indeed light, and they are upon pulpits of light. They do not fear when people fear, and they do not grieve when people grieve." Then he recited: ﴿Unquestionably, the friends of Allah—there is no fear for them, nor shall they grieve.﴾

Ali ibn Abi Talib (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "The friends of Allah are a people whose faces are pale from staying awake at night, whose eyes are sunken from reflection, whose stomachs are hollow from hunger, and whose lips are dry from thirst [[dhawi al-ʿawd wa-l-ʿaql yadhwa dhayan wa-dhuwiyyan: both mean it withered and dried out; a thing is dhaw when it does not receive moisture, or the heat strikes it so that it wilts and weakens.]]."

It was also said: "There is no fear for them" regarding their offspring, because Allah takes care of them. "Nor shall they grieve" over their worldly possessions, because Allah compensates them in this life and the next, since He is their Protector and their Master.

This is the description of the friends of Allah, the Exalted. So "alladhina" (those who) is in the accusative position as a substitute (badal) for the noun of "inna," which is "awliya'" (friends). And if you wish, it may be read as accusative by an implied "a'ni" (I mean). It was also said: it is a beginning (mubtada'), and its predicate is:

﴿They shall have good tidings in the life of this world and in the Hereafter﴾

Then it is cut off from what precedes it, meaning: they guard against shirk (associating partners with Allah) and sins.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 10, verse 64:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿For them is good news in the life of this world﴾

From Abu al-Darda', who said: I asked the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) about it, and he said: "No one has asked me about it besides you since it was revealed. It is the good dream that a Muslim sees, or that is seen for him." Related by al-Tirmidhi in his Jami'.

Al-Zuhri, 'Ata' and Qatadah said: It is the good news that the angels give the believer in this world at the time of death.

From Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi, who said: When the soul of the believing servant becomes stirred up [[i.e., when it gathers in him, wishing to leave, just as water collects in its bed. By "soul" he means the spirit. (Ibn al-Athir).]], the Angel of Death comes to him and says: "Peace be upon you, friend of Allah. Allah sends you His greeting." Then he recited this verse: ﴿Those whom the angels take in death while they are good, saying: Peace be upon you﴾ [[See vol. 10, p. 100 and what follows.]] [al-Nahl: 32]. Recorded by Ibn al-Mubarak.

Qatadah and al-Dahhak said: It is that he knows where he will be before he dies.

Al-Hasan said: It is what Allah, exalted is He, gives them good news of in His Book, of His Garden and His generous reward, based on His saying: ﴿Their Lord gives them good news of mercy from Him and approval﴾ [[See p. 93 of this volume.]] [al-Tawbah: 21], and His saying: ﴿And give good news to those who believe and do righteous deeds that for them are gardens﴾ [[See vol. 1, p. 237 and what follows.]] [al-Baqarah: 25], and His saying: ﴿And rejoice in the Garden which you were promised﴾ [[See vol. 15, p. 357.]] [Fussilat: 30]. And for this reason He said: ﴿There is no changing of the words of Allah﴾, meaning there is no breaking of His promises, because His promises are His words.

(In the Hereafter) It was said: with the Garden when they come out of their graves. It was also said: when the spirit departs, it is given good news of the approval of Allah. Abu Ishaq al-Tha'labi mentioned: I heard Abu Bakr Muhammad ibn Abd Allah al-Jawzaqi [[This nisba is to Jawzaq (on the pattern of Ja'far), a town in Nishapur.]] say: I saw Abu Abd Allah al-Hafiz in a dream, riding a horse with a shawl and a turban on him. I greeted him and said to him: Welcome to you! We never cease to mention you and to mention your virtues. He said: And we never cease to mention you and to mention your virtues. Allah the Exalted says: "For them is good news in the life of this world and in the Hereafter." Good praise. And he gestured with his hand.

﴿There is no changing of the words of Allah﴾, meaning there is no breaking of His promise. It was also said: there is no altering of His reports, meaning He will not abrogate them with anything, and they will only be as He said.

﴿That is the great triumph﴾, meaning what His friends come to is the great triumph.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 10, verse 65:

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And let not their speech grieve you﴾, then the speech is complete, meaning: let not their fabrication and their denial of you grieve you. Then he began and said: "Indeed, all might (al-izza) belongs to Allah", meaning the complete strength, the all-encompassing dominance and the perfect power belong to Allah alone. So He is your Helper, your Supporter and your Protector.

"Jamee'an" (all together) is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal). This is not contradicted by His words: ﴿But might belongs to Allah, to His Messenger and to the believers﴾ [al-Munafiqun: 8] [[See vol. 18, p. 129.]], because every might is through Allah, so all of it belongs to Allah. Allah the Glorified says: ﴿Glory be to your Lord, the Lord of might, above what they describe﴾ [as-Saffat: 180] [[See vol. 15, p. 140.]].

﴿He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing﴾: All-Hearing of their words and their voices, All-Knowing of their deeds, their actions and all their movements.

Allah's words: ﴿Unquestionably, to Allah belongs whoever is in the heavens and whoever is on the earth﴾, meaning He judges concerning them as He wills, and does with them whatever He pleases, glory be to Him!

Allah's words: (And those who call upon other than Allah do not follow partners.) "Mā" here is for negation, meaning they do not truly follow partners; rather they assume that they intercede or benefit. It was also said that "mā" is interrogative, meaning: what do those who call upon other than Allah follow as partners? This is a condemnation of their act. Then He answered, saying: ﴿They follow nothing but assumption, and they are only guessing﴾, meaning they conjecture and lie. This has already been discussed [[see vol. 7, p. 71.]].

He said, may He be exalted: ﴿It is He who made the night for you that you might rest therein﴾. This shows that what is obligatory is worship of the One who is able to create the night and the day, not worship of one who has no power over anything. "That you might rest therein": that is, with your spouses and your children, so that weariness and exhaustion may leave you. And al-sukun (rest) is stillness, the calm that is the opposite of agitation.

He said, may He be exalted: ﴿and the day to see by﴾, meaning illuminated, so that you may be guided by it in your needs. Al-mubsir is that which gives sight, and the day is seen by means of it. He said "mubsiran" (seeing) as a figurative extension and broadening, following the Arabs' custom in such phrases as "a standing night" (laylun qa'im) and "a fasting day" (naharun sa'im). Jarir said:

"You blamed us, O Umm Ghaylan, for travelling by night,
and you slept, while the night of the riding camels does not sleep."

Qutrub said: "Aẓlama al-layl" means the night became dark, that is, it became possessed of darkness; "wa-adā'a al-nahar wa-abṣara" means the day became radiant, that is, it became possessed of light and sight.

He said, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed in that are signs﴾, meaning indications and evidences.

(﴿for a people who hear﴾), meaning hearing with reflection.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 10, verse 68:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They say, "Allah has taken a son."﴾ meaning the disbelievers. This has already been mentioned [[See vol. 2, p. 85.]].

(Subhanahu) He has declared Himself exempt from companions, offspring, associates, and rivals.

(﴿He is the Self-Sufficient; to Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth.﴾) Then He informed of His absolute self-sufficiency, and that to Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and the earth, in ownership, creation, and servitude: ﴿There is none in the heavens and the earth but that he comes to the Most Merciful as a servant.﴾ [[See vol. 11, p. 155.]] [Maryam: 93].

(﴿You have no authority for this.﴾) That is, you have no proof for this.

(﴿Do you say about Allah what you do not know?﴾) Namely, attributing a son to Him. A son implies kinship and resemblance, whereas Allah, exalted is He, does not share kinship with anything, nor does He resemble anything.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 10, verse 69–70:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Say: Indeed, those who invent lies against Allah﴾, i.e., who fabricate them.

(They will not succeed in falsehood against Allah) i.e., they will not win and will not be safe. And the statement is complete.

(A brief enjoyment in this world) i.e., that is an enjoyment, or it is an enjoyment in the world. This was said by al-Kisa'i. Al-Akhfash said: For them is an enjoyment in the world. Abu Ishaq said: In other than the Qur'an, the accusative (naṣb) is permissible, in the sense of "they enjoy an enjoyment" (yatamatta'una mata'an).

(Then to Us is their return) i.e., their return.

(Then We will make them taste the severe punishment) i.e., the harsh one.

(Because they used to disbelieve) i.e., because of their disbelief.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 10, verse 69–70:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Say: Indeed, those who invent lies against Allah﴾, i.e., who fabricate them.

(They will not succeed in falsehood against Allah) i.e., they will not win and will not be safe. And the statement is complete.

(A brief enjoyment in this world) i.e., that is an enjoyment, or it is an enjoyment in the world. This was said by al-Kisa'i. Al-Akhfash said: For them is an enjoyment in the world. Abu Ishaq said: In other than the Qur'an, the accusative (naṣb) is permissible, in the sense of "they enjoy an enjoyment" (yatamatta'una mata'an).

(Then to Us is their return) i.e., their return.

(Then We will make them taste the severe punishment) i.e., the harsh one.

(Because they used to disbelieve) i.e., because of their disbelief.

The Lord, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And recite to them the report of Noah﴾. He, peace be upon him, was commanded to remind them of the stories of earlier peoples and to warn them of the painful punishment for their disbelief. The waw was dropped from "اتْلُ" (recite) because it is an imperative, meaning: recite to them the account of Noah.

(When he said to his people) "إِذْ" (when) is in the accusative position.

(O my people, if my standing [among you] and my reminding you of the signs of God has been burdensome to you) meaning: if it has been great and heavy upon you.

(my standing) "الْمَقَامُ" with a fatha on the mim means the place where one stands. "الْمُقَامُ" with a damma means staying. To my knowledge, it was not read with a damma. The meaning is: if my remaining among you has been long for you.

(and my reminding you) and my warning you.

(of the signs of God) and you have resolved to kill me and drive me out.

(then in God I have put my trust) meaning: I have relied upon Him. This is the answer to the conditional clause. He, peace be upon him, was always trusting in God in every situation, but he made clear that he was trusting in this matter in particular, so that his people would know that God would suffice him against their affair. In other words: if you do not help me, I trust in the One who will help me.

The Lord, Exalted is He, said: "(So resolve upon your affair, and [gather] your associates)." The reading of the common majority is "فَأَجْمِعُوا" with an initial hamza cut, and "شُرَكاءَكُمْ" in the accusative. ['Asim al-Jahdari read "فَاجْمَعُوا" with a connected alif and a fatha on the mim, from جَمَعَ يَجْمَعُ, and "شُرَكاءَكُمْ" in the accusative. Al-Hasan, Ibn Abi Ishaq and Ya'qub read "فَأَجْمِعُوا" with a cut hamza and "شُرَكَاؤُكُمْ" in the nominative.] As for the first reading, it is from أَجْمَعَ عَلَى الشَّيْءِ, meaning to resolve upon something. Al-Farra' said: أَجْمَعَ الشَّيْءَ means to prepare it. Al-Mu'arrij said: "أَجْمَعْتُ الْأَمْرَ" is more eloquent than "أَجْمَعْتُ عَلَيْهِ". He recited:

"Would that I knew, while wishes do not benefit, whether I will go forth one day with my affair resolved."

Al-Nahhas said: On this reading, the accusative of "الشُّرَكَاءَ" has three possible explanations. Al-Kisa'i and al-Farra' said: it means "and call upon your associates to help you," and it is accusative for them by implying this verb. Muhammad ibn Yazid [al-Mubarrad] said: it is coordinated with the meaning, as in the poet's words:

"Would that your spouse in battle were girded with a sword and a spear."

The spear is not girded, but it is carried like the sword. Abu Ishaq al-Zajjaj said: the meaning is "together with your associates in your mutual support," as one says: "the water met the wood." The second reading is from جَمَعَ, based on the Lord's saying: ﴿So he gathered his plot, then came﴾ [Ta-Ha: 60]. Abu Mu'adh said: it is possible that جَمَعَ and أَجْمَعَ have the same meaning. On this reading, "وَشُرَكاءَكُمْ" is coordinated with "أَمْرَكُمْ", or [it means] "resolve your affair and resolve your associates," or, if you wish, it means "with" (مع). Abu Ja'far al-Nahhas said: I heard Abu Ishaq permit "قَامَ زَيْدٌ وَعَمْرًا" (Zayd stood, and 'Amr [too]). The third reading is that the associates are coordinated with the pronoun in "أَجْمِعُوا" (the subject you), and this is good because the speech has been lengthened. Al-Nahhas and others said: this reading is weak, because if it were nominative it would have to be written with a waw, and no waw appears in the codices in "وَشُرَكاءَكُمْ". Also, their associates are idols, and idols do nothing and have no action, so they cannot be gathered. Al-Mahdawi said: it is possible that "الشُّرَكَاءُ" is nominative as a subject, with the predicate omitted, meaning "and your associates, let them gather their affair." This is attributed to the associates, although they neither hear, see nor discern, as a rebuke to those who worship them.

The Lord, Exalted is He, said: ﴿Then let not your affair be obscured to you﴾. "غُمَّةً" is the predicate of "يَكُنْ" and its subject is "أَمْرُكُمْ". "غُمَّة" and "غَمٌّ" are the same, and its meaning is covering, from their saying: "غُمَّ الْهِلَالُ" when the crescent is hidden. The meaning: let your affair be clear and manifest, so that you can act as you wish in it, not like one whose affair is concealed so that he cannot achieve what he desires. Tarafa said:

"By your life, my affair is not hidden from me, neither my day nor my night is perpetual over me."

Al-Zajjaj said: "غُمَّةٌ" is "ذَا غَمٍّ" (possessing distress), and الْغَمُّ and الْغُمَّةُ are like الْكَرْبُ and الْكُرْبَةُ (both meaning distress). It was said: "الْغُمَّةُ" is the narrowness of the affair that causes distress, so that its owner cannot discern a way out of it, so that what distresses him may be relieved. In al-Sihah: "الْغُمَّةُ" is anguish. Al-'Ajjaj said:

"Indeed, if you had witnessed the people when they were covered with distress, had it not been relieved, you would have been distressed."

One says: أَمْرٌ غُمَّةٌ, meaning an affair that is ambiguous and confused. The Lord, Exalted is He, said: "Then let not your affair be obscured to you." Abu 'Ubayda said: its figurative sense is darkness and constriction. "الْغُمَّةُ" also means the bottom of a "نِحْي" (a jar for ghee) and other things. Others said: the root of all this derives from الْغَمَامَةُ (the cloud).

The Lord, Exalted is He, said: ﴿Then carry out your decision against me and give me no respite﴾. The alif of "اقْضُوا" is an alif of connection, from قَضَى يَقْضِي. Al-Akhfash and al-Kisa'i said: it is like the Lord's saying: ﴿And We decreed that matter to him﴾ [al-Hijr: 66], meaning: We conveyed it to him and communicated it to him. It is related from Ibn 'Abbas regarding "ثُمَّ اقْضُوا إِلَيَّ وَلا تُنْظِرُونِ" that he said: proceed against me and do not delay. Al-Nahhas said: this is a sound statement in the language, and from it comes قَضَى الْمَيِّتُ, meaning the dead one passed away. By this he informed them that they would not reach him, and this is among the proofs of prophethood. Al-Farra' transmitted from some readers "ثُمَّ أَفْضُوا إِلَيَّ" with a fa and a cut hamza, meaning: turn towards me, as one says: أَفْضَتِ الْخِلَافَةُ إِلَى فُلَانٍ (the caliphate devolved upon so-and-so) and أَفْضَى إِلَيَّ الْوَجَعُ (the pain reached me). This is a report from God, Exalted is He, about His Prophet Noah, peace be upon him, that he was confident in God's help and not afraid of their plotting, knowing that they and their gods neither benefit nor harm. It is a consolation to His Prophet ﷺ and a strengthening of his heart.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿But if you turn away, then I have not asked you for any reward﴾, meaning: if you turn away from what I have brought you, that is not because I asked you for a wage, so that my recompense would weigh heavily upon you.

﴿My reward is only with Allah﴾ in conveying His message.

﴿And I have been commanded to be among the Muslims﴾, meaning among those who affirm the oneness of Allah the Exalted. The people of Madinah, Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir and Hafs read the yā' of "ajriya" wherever it occurs as a long vowel (fatḥ-based, "ajriya"), while the rest read it with sukūn ("ajri").

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 10, verse 73:

Allah the Exalted's words: ﴿But they denied him﴾ meaning Noah.

(So We delivered him and those with him) i.e., of the believers.

(In the ark) i.e., the ship (al-fulk), and its mention will come.

(And We made them successors) i.e., the inhabitants of the earth and successors to those who were drowned.

(So see how was the end of those who were warned) meaning the final outcome of those whom the messengers warned but who did not believe.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 10, verse 74:

Allah's statement: ﴿Then We sent after him﴾ i.e., after Nuh (Noah).

(Messengers to their peoples) such as Hud, Salih, Ibrahim, Lut, Shu'ayb and others.

(And they brought them clear proofs) i.e., with the miracles (mu'jizat).

(But they would not have believed in what they had denied before.)

The estimated meaning: "in what the people of Nuh had denied before." It was also said: "in what they had denied before" means before the Day of the Covenant (yawm al-dharr), for among them were those who denied in their hearts even though they all said: "Yes" (balaa). An-Nahhas said: "One of the best things said about this is that it refers to specific people, like: ﴿It is the same for them whether you warn them or do not warn them; they will not believe﴾ [al-Baqarah: 6]." (Thus We seal) i.e., We set a seal.

(upon the hearts of the transgressors) i.e., those who exceed the limit in disbelief and denial, so that they do not believe. This refutes the Qadariyyah in their statement, as has already been mentioned.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 10, verse 75:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then after them We sent﴾, meaning: after the messengers and the nations (before them).

(Musa and Harun to Pharaoh and his chiefs) meaning: the nobles of his people.

(with Our signs) he means the nine signs, and their mention has already preceded [[See vol. 2, p. 30, and vol. 7, p. 267.]].

(But they were arrogant) meaning: towards the truth.

(And they were a guilty people) meaning: polytheists.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 10, verse 76–77:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So when the truth came to them from Us﴾, he means Pharaoh and his people. (﴿They said, "Indeed, this is clear magic."﴾) They took the miracles to be magic. Musa said to them: ﴿Do you say of the truth when it has come to you, "Is this magic?" And magicians do not succeed.﴾ It has been said that there is an ellipsis in the speech; the meaning is: "Do you say of the truth, 'This is magic'?" So "Do you say" is a rebuke, and their saying is omitted, i.e., "This is magic," and then he resumed with another rebuke from his side, saying: "Is this magic?" He omitted their first saying, being satisfied with the second part of their saying, denouncing Pharaoh and his chiefs. Al-Akhfash said: it is from their saying, and the alif entered as a quotation of their saying, because they said, "Is this magic?" So it was said to them: "Do you say of the truth when it has come to you, 'Is this magic?'" This is narrated from al-Hasan.

(﴿And magicians do not succeed﴾) i.e., whoever brings it does not succeed.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 10, verse 76–77:

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿So when the truth came to them from Us﴾, he means Pharaoh and his people. (﴿They said, "Indeed, this is clear magic."﴾) They took the miracles to be magic. Musa said to them: ﴿Do you say of the truth when it has come to you, "Is this magic?" And magicians do not succeed.﴾ It has been said that there is an ellipsis in the speech; the meaning is: "Do you say of the truth, 'This is magic'?" So "Do you say" is a rebuke, and their saying is omitted, i.e., "This is magic," and then he resumed with another rebuke from his side, saying: "Is this magic?" He omitted their first saying, being satisfied with the second part of their saying, denouncing Pharaoh and his chiefs. Al-Akhfash said: it is from their saying, and the alif entered as a quotation of their saying, because they said, "Is this magic?" So it was said to them: "Do you say of the truth when it has come to you, 'Is this magic?'" This is narrated from al-Hasan.

(﴿And magicians do not succeed﴾) i.e., whoever brings it does not succeed.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 10, verse 78:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿They said: "Have you come to us to turn us away﴾ — i.e., to divert us and twist us. It is said: lafatahu yalfituhu laftan, meaning he twisted him and turned him away. The poet said:

I turned toward the tribe until I saw myself... and I was pained from the listening, in the neck and the vein [of the neck].

[The verse is by al-Summa al-Qushayri. al-Isgha' means inclination. al-Layt (with a kasra) is the side of the neck. al-Akhda' is a vein in the side of the neck.]

And from this comes "iltafata" (he turned), which is simply to deviate from the direction that is in front of him.

(﴿from what we found our fathers following﴾) — he means the worship of idols.

(﴿and that greatness may be yours﴾) — i.e., magnificence, dominion and authority.

(﴿in the land﴾) — he means the land of Egypt. And dominion is called al-kibriya' (greatness) because it is the greatest thing sought in this world. ﴿And we are not believers in you both.﴾ Ibn Mas'ud, al-Hasan and others read "wayakunu" with the ya', because the feminine here is not real (haqiqi) and a separation has occurred between them. Sibawayh related: "hadara al-qadi al-yawma imra'atan" (the judge came today, two women).

He said it only when he saw the staff and the white hand and believed that they were sorcery. Hamza, al-Kisa'i, Ibn Wathhab and al-A'mash read "سَحَّارٍ" (*sahhar*, an intensive form meaning "a great sorcerer"). The discussion of these two readings has already been given in al-A'raf [[See vol. 7, p. 257 onward.]].
That is, throw on the ground whatever you have with you of your ropes and your staffs. The matter has already been discussed fully in al-A'raf [see vol. 7, p. 257 and following].

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 10, verse 81:

The words of the Exalted: ﴿When they had cast, Moses said, "What you have brought is magic."﴾ The word *mā* (ما) may be in the nominative position as the grammatical subject (*mubtada'*), with the predicate (*khabar*) being *ji'tum bihi* (جئتم به), "you brought it." The sense is: *ayyu shay'in ji'tum bihi* (أي شيء جئتم به), "what thing did you bring?", in rebuke and belittlement of what they had brought of magic.

Abu 'Amr's reading is *ālsiḥru* (آلسحر), in interrogative form, with an implied subject, the sense being: *ahuwa al-siḥr* (أهو السحر), "is it magic?" It is also permissible for it to be the subject with the predicate omitted, the sense being: *al-siḥru ji'tum bihi* (السحر جئتم به), "magic is what you brought."

When the reader uses the interrogative reading, *mā* cannot mean "that which" (*alladhī*), since it would have no predicate. The rest of the readers read *al-siḥru* (السحر) as a predicate. The evidence for this reading is the reading of Ibn Mas'ud: "What you have brought is magic" (*mā ji'tum bihi siḥrun*, ما جئتم به سحر). The reading of Ubayy is: "What you have brought is magic" (*mā ataytum bihi siḥrun*, ما أتيتم به سحر). Here *mā* means "that which" (*alladhī*), *ji'tum bihi* (جئتم به) is the relative clause (*ṣilah*), the position of *mā* is nominative as subject (*mubtada'*), and *al-siḥru* is the predicate of the subject. When *mā* is taken to mean "that which," it cannot be in the accusative, because the relative clause does not govern the relative pronoun.

Al-Farra' permitted the accusative *al-siḥra* (السحر) governed by *ji'tum* (جئتم). In that case *mā* is a conditional particle (*shart*), *ji'tum* is in the jussive position governed by *mā*, and the response (*jawab*) is elided with its *fa'* (فاء), the sense being: *fa-inna Allāha sayubṭiluhu* (فإن الله سيبطله), "then God will nullify it." It is also permissible for *al-siḥra* to be in the accusative as a verbal noun (*maṣdar*), the sense being: *mā ji'tum bihi siḥran* (ما جئتم به سحرا), "what you have brought is magic," and then the definite article *al-* (الألف واللام) is added as an extra element. On this reading there is no need to elide the *fa'*. Al-Nahhas chose this view and said: The omission of the *fa'* in conditional constructions is not permitted by many grammarians except in poetic necessity, as in the verse:

*Man yafʿalu al-ḥasanāti Allāhu yashkuruhā*
(مَنْ يَفْعَلُ الْحَسَنَاتِ اللَّهُ يَشْكُرُهَا)
Whoever does good deeds, God will reward them.

Some even said that it is not permitted at all. I heard 'Ali ibn Sulayman say: Muhammad ibn Yazid narrated to me, saying: al-Mazini narrated to me, saying: I heard al-Asma'i say: The grammarians altered this line, and the actual transmission is:

*Man yafʿalu al-khayra fa-al-Raḥmānu yashkuruhu*
(مَنْ يَفْعَلُ الْخَيْرَ فَالرَّحْمَنُ يَشْكُرُهُ)
Whoever does good, the Most Merciful will reward him.

I heard 'Ali ibn Sulayman say: Omitting the *fa'* in conditional constructions is permissible. He said: The evidence for this is the verse: ﴿Whatever affliction befalls you is because of what your own hands have earned﴾ [[See vol. 16, p. 30.]]. The reading "*wa-mā aṣābakum min muṣībatin fa-bimā kasabat aydīkum*" (وما أصابكم من مصيبة فبما كسبت أيديكم) has two well-known and established readings.

﴿Indeed, God does not set right the work of the corrupters﴾, meaning the magic. Ibn 'Abbas said: Whoever takes his bed at night and then recites this verse [...].

﴿What you have brought is magic; indeed God will nullify it. Indeed, God does not set right the work of the corrupters﴾ [...] No magician's scheme will harm him, and it will not be cast upon one who is bewitched except that God will repel the magic from him.

[[In manuscript 'a': "wa-rubbamā" (and perhaps).]]

Allah's words: ﴿And Allah will establish the truth﴾, meaning He will make it manifest and clarify it.

(by His words) meaning by His speech, His proofs and His evidences. It was also said: by His promises of victory.

(even though the criminals dislike it) meaning the criminals from the family of Pharaoh.

**Al-Qurtubi's commentary (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Qur'an) on Surah 10, verse 83:**

Allah's words: ﴿But none believed in Musa except some offspring of his people﴾. The pronoun in "his people" refers back to Musa.

Mujahid said: That is, none of them (the people of Pharaoh) believed. Only the descendants of the Children of Israel to whom Musa was sent believed. Over the long passage of time, the fathers died and the sons remained, and they believed. This is the view chosen by al-Tabari. The word *dhurriyyah* (offspring, descendants) refers to a person's later generations, and it may be numerous.

It was also said that by *dhurriyyah* he meant the believers among the Children of Israel. Ibn Abbas said: They were six hundred thousand, because Ya'qub (peace be upon him) entered Egypt (Misr) with seventy-two persons, and they multiplied in Egypt until they reached six hundred thousand.

Ibn Abbas also said: "from his people" means from the people of Pharaoh (Fir'awn). Among them were the believer from the family of Pharaoh, Pharaoh's treasurer, his wife, the hairdresser of his daughter, and the wife of his treasurer.

It was also said: they are people whose fathers were from the Copts and whose mothers were from the Children of Israel, so they were called *dhurriyyah*, just as the sons of the Persians who multiplied in Yemen and the lands of the Arabs are called *abna'* (sons), because their mothers were not of the same kind as their fathers. This was stated by al-Farra'. On this view, the pronoun in "his people" refers to Musa because of kinship through the mothers, and to Pharaoh if they were from the Copts.

Allah's words: ﴿out of fear of Pharaoh﴾, because he was dominant over them and a tyrant.

﴿And their chiefs﴾: he said *mala'ihim* (their chiefs) and did not say *mala'ihi* (his chiefs). On this there are six answers:

The first: since Pharaoh was a tyrant, the verb was reported about him in the plural, as an expression of the whole group.

The second: when Pharaoh was mentioned, it was understood that others were with him, so the pronoun returned to him and to them. This is one of the two views of al-Farra'.

The third: the group was named after Pharaoh, as Thamud is named after its ancestor.

The fourth: the implied meaning is "out of fear of the family of Pharaoh," so this is an instance of omitting a noun that is annexed (*hadhf al-mudaf*), as in ﴿And ask the town﴾ [Yusuf: 82]. This is the second view of al-Farra'. However, this answer is wrong according to the school of Sibawayh and al-Khalil, who do not permit "Hind stood up" when you mean "her servant" (i.e., the verb agreeing with the name when the meaning is of a different person).

The fifth: the view of al-Akhfash Sa'id is that the pronoun returns to the offspring (*dhurriyyah*), meaning the chiefs of the offspring. This is the choice of al-Tabari.

The sixth: the pronoun returns to "his people." Al-Nahhas said: This answer is apparently the most eloquent of them.

Allah's words: ﴿that he would persecute them﴾. He used the singular *yaftinahum* (he would persecute them) in reporting about Pharaoh, meaning that he would turn them away from their religion by punishments. The phrase is in the genitive position (*khafd*) as a partial substitution (*badal ishtimal*, a substitute that includes what it replaces). It may also be in the accusative position, governed by "fear" (*khawf*).

Pharaoh is not declined (*lam yanṣarif*) because it is a non-Arabic (*a'jami*) proper name and it is definite.

Allah's words: ﴿Indeed Pharaoh was haughty in the land﴾, that is, he was overbearing and arrogant. ﴿And indeed he was among the transgressors﴾, that is, those who exceed the limit in disbelief, because he was a slave who claimed lordship.

"And Moses said, 'O my people, if you have believed in God, then rely upon Him, if you are Muslims.'" (Qur'an 10:84)

(If you have believed in God) means: if you have affirmed (sadaqtum) [the truth].

(Then rely upon Him) means: depend upon Him (i'timadu).

(If you are Muslims) he repeated the condition for emphasis, and made clear that the perfection of faith lies in entrusting the matter to God.

(So they said, "In God we have put our trust.") means: we have surrendered our affairs to Him, we are content with His decree and His destiny, and we submit to His command.

("Our Lord, do not make us a trial for the wrongdoing people.") means: do not let them prevail over us, for that would be a trial for us regarding the religion; or, do not test us by having us punished at their hands. Mujahid said: the meaning is, do not destroy us by the hands of our enemies, nor punish us with a punishment from You, so that our enemies would say, "Had they been upon the truth, we would not have been given power over them," and thus they would be tempted. Abu Mijlaz and Abu al-Duha said: it means, do not let them overcome us, so that they would see that they are better than us and thereby increase in their transgression.

"And Moses said, 'O my people, if you have believed in God, then rely upon Him, if you are Muslims.'" (Qur'an 10:84)

(If you have believed in God) means: if you have affirmed (sadaqtum) [the truth].

(Then rely upon Him) means: depend upon Him (i'timadu).

(So they said, "In God we have put our trust.") means: we have surrendered our affairs to Him, we are content with His decree and His destiny, and we submit to His command.

("Our Lord, do not make us a trial for the wrongdoing people.") means: do not let them prevail over us, for that would be a trial for us regarding the religion; or, do not test us by having us punished at their hands. Mujahid said: the meaning is, do not destroy us by the hands of our enemies, nor punish us with a punishment from You, so that our enemies would say, "Had they been upon the truth, we would not have been given power over them," and thus they would be tempted.
