Al-Qurtubi's commentary on verse 10:86:

His saying, may He exalt Him: ﴿And save us by Your mercy﴾, meaning: deliver us.

(From the disbelieving people) meaning: from Pharaoh and his people, because they used to subject them to heavy labour.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 10, verse 87:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We revealed to Musa and his brother: "Settle your people in Egypt in houses"﴾. In this there are five issues.

The first: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We revealed to Musa and his brother that you should settle﴾, i.e., take [for yourselves]. "for your people in Egypt, houses." It is said: "I settled Zayd in a place" (bawwa'tu Zaydan makanan) and "I settled for Zayd a place" (bawwa'tu li-Zaydin makanan). The mubawwa' is the lodging that is held fast, and from it comes "Allah settled him in a dwelling" (bawwa'ahu Allahu manzilan), i.e., made him keep to it and made him dwell in it. From it is the hadith: "Whoever lies about me deliberately, let him take his seat in the Fire" (fal-yatabawwa' maq'adahu mina al-nar). The rajaz poet said:

"We are the sons of 'Adnan, there is no doubt... Glory and kingship have settled among us."

Misr (Egypt) in this verse is Alexandria, according to Mujahid. Al-Dahhak said: it is the land called Misr, and Misr extends from the sea to Aswan, and Alexandria is part of the land of Egypt.

The second: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And make your houses a qiblah﴾. Most of the exegetes said: the Children of Israel did not pray except in their places of worship and churches, and these were conspicuous. When Musa was sent, Pharaoh ordered that the places of worship of the Children of Israel be destroyed, and all of them were ruined and they were prevented from prayer. So Allah revealed to Musa and Harun: "Take for the Children of Israel houses in Egypt," i.e., places of worship (masajid), and He did not intend inhabited dwellings. This is the saying of Ibrahim, Ibn Zayd, al-Rabi', Abu Malik, Ibn 'Abbas and others. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas and Sa'id ibn Jubayr that the meaning is: "make your houses face one another." The first view is more sound, i.e., make your places of worship face the qiblah. It was said: Bayt al-Maqdis, and it is the qiblah of the Jews to this day, as said by Ibn Bahr. It was also said: the Ka'bah. From Ibn 'Abbas who said: the Ka'bah was the qiblah of Musa and those with him. This indicates that the qiblah in prayer was a legislated matter for Musa, peace be upon him, and prayer was not free of the conditions of purity, covering the nakedness, and facing the qiblah, for that is more effective in obligation and more abundant in worship. It was also said: the meaning is "pray in your houses secretly, so that you may be safe," and that was when Pharaoh frightened them; so they were commanded to be patient, to take places of worship in their houses, to proceed to prayer, and to supplicate until Allah fulfils His promise. This is what is meant by His saying: "Musa said to his people: Seek help in Allah and be patient" [see vol. 7, p. 261 onward], and the verse. It was part of their religion that they did not pray except in the synagogues and churches while they were in safety; but when they feared, they were permitted to pray in their houses. Ibn al-'Arabi said: the first of the two views is more apparent, because the second is a claim. I say: his saying "a claim" is correct, for in the Sahih is the saying of the Prophet, peace be upon him: "The earth has been made for me a mosque and a means of purification," and this is among what he was singled out with over the prophets. So we, praise be to Allah, pray in the mosques and in the houses, wherever the prayer overtakes us; except that voluntary prayer in the homes is better than in the mosques, even the rak'ah before and after the Friday prayer, and before and after the obligatory prayers, since voluntary prayers may be affected by showing off (riya'), whereas obligatory prayers are not; and whenever the deed is free of showing off, it is heavier and nearer to Allah, glory be to Him and exalted is He. Muslim related from 'Abd Allah ibn Shaqiq who said: I asked 'A'ishah about the prayer of the Messenger of Allah ﷺ in terms of his voluntary prayers. She said: "He used to pray in my house four rak'ahs before the Dhuhr, then he would go out and lead the people in prayer, then he would enter and pray two rak'ahs, and he used to lead the people in the Maghrib, then he would enter and pray two rak'ahs, then he would lead the people in the 'Isha', and he would enter my house and pray two rak'ahs..." (the hadith). And from Ibn 'Umar who said: I prayed with the Prophet ﷺ two prostrations before the Dhuhr and two after it, and two after the Maghrib; as for the Maghrib, 'Isha' and Friday, I prayed with the Prophet ﷺ in his house. Abu Dawud related from Ka'b ibn 'Ujrah that the Prophet ﷺ came to the mosque of Banu al-Ashhal and prayed the Maghrib in it; when they finished their prayer he saw them glorifying Allah after it, and he said: "This is the prayer of the houses."

The third: The scholars differed in this chapter concerning the night prayer of Ramadan (qiyam Ramadan): is performing it in the house better, or in the mosque? Malik held that it is better in the house for one who is able to do so, and Abu Yusuf said likewise, as did some companions of al-Shafi'i. Ibn 'Abd al-Hakam, Ahmad and some companions of al-Shafi'i held that attending it in congregation is better. Al-Layth said: if people stood [in prayer] in their houses and no one stood in the mosque, they should not go out to it. The proof for Malik and those who agree with him is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ in the hadith of Zayd ibn Thabit: "So keep to praying in your houses, for the best prayer of a person is in his house, except the obligatory prayer," related by al-Bukhari. The opponent argued that the Prophet ﷺ prayed it in congregation in the mosque, then informed of the obstacle that prevented him from persisting in that, which was the fear that it would be made obligatory upon them; therefore he said to them: "So keep to praying in your houses." Then the Companions used to pray it in the mosque in scattered groups, until 'Umar gathered them behind a single reciter, and the matter became settled upon that and was established as a sunnah.

The fourth: If we accept that it was permitted to them to pray in their houses when they feared for their lives, then it is taken as evidence that one who is excused by fear or otherwise may leave the congregation and the Friday prayer. The excuse that permits this is like a restraining illness, or fear of its increase, or fear of the oppression of a ruler regarding property or body, short of a judgment against him in a matter of right. Heavy rain with mud is an excuse if it does not cease, and one who has a close relative who is near death and has no one to nurse him; Ibn 'Umar did so.

The fifth: His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And give good tidings to the believers﴾. It was said: the address is to Muhammad ﷺ. It was also said: to Musa, peace be upon him, and this is more apparent, i.e., give the Children of Israel good tidings that Allah will make them victorious over their enemy.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 10, verse 88:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And Moses said, "Our Lord, indeed You have given Pharaoh and his chiefs"﴾. "Ataita" means "You gave."

(adornment and wealth in the life of this world): that is, the wealth of this world. They possessed, from the Fustat of Egypt to the land of Abyssinia, mountains containing mines of gold, silver, zabarjad (chrysolite), zumurrud (emerald), and yaqut (ruby).

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿"Our Lord, so that they may lead astray from Your way"﴾. Scholars have differed concerning this lam (the particle "li"), and the most sound of what has been said about it, which is the view of al-Khalil and Sibawayh, is that it is the lam of consequence and outcome (lam al-'aqibah wa al-sayrurah). In a report: "Indeed, Allah the Exalted has an angel who calls out every day: 'Give birth for death, and build for ruin.'" That is, since the outcome of their affair was to misguidance, it became as though He had given them so that they would go astray. It has also been said that it is the lam of purpose (lam kay), meaning: You gave them so that they would go astray, become arrogant and act haughtily. It has also been said that it is the lam of cause (lam ajl), meaning: You gave them because of their turning away from You, so they did not fear that You would turn away from them. Some people claimed that the meaning is: You gave them that so that they would not go astray, and the particle (la, negation) was omitted, as the Mighty and Majestic said: ﴿Allah makes clear to you, lest you go astray﴾ [4:176] (see vol. 6, p. 28 onward). And the meaning is: "so that you do not go astray." Al-Nahhas said: The apparent sense of this answer is good, except that the Arabs do not omit "la" except together with "an," so the proponent of this answer blurred the point with His saying, Mighty and Majestic: "an tadillu" (that you go astray). It has also been said: the lam is for supplication, meaning: test them with straying from Your way, because after it comes: "Obliterate their wealth and harden their hearts." It has also been said: the verb carries the sense of the verbal noun, meaning "their leading astray," as in the saying of the Mighty and Majestic: ﴿to turn away from them﴾ [9:63]. The Kufans read "liyudillu" with a damma on the ya' from the form of ighwa' (ilal), while the rest read it with a fatha.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿"Our Lord, obliterate their wealth"﴾: that is, punish them for their disbelief by destroying their wealth. Al-Zajjaj said: tamsu al-shay' means removing it from its form. Ibn 'Abbas and Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: their wealth and their dirhams became carved stones in the same shapes as they were, whole, thirds and halves, and no mine remained to them except that Allah obliterated it, so no one benefited from it afterwards. Qatadah said: it has reached us that their wealth and their crops became stones. Mujahid and 'Atiyyah said: He destroyed it so that it could not be seen; it is said "a obliterated eye" (ayn matmusah), and "the place was obliterated" (tumisa al-mawdi') when it was effaced and obliterated. Ibn Zayd said: their dinars, their dirhams, their furnishings, and everything that belonged to them became stones. Muhammad ibn Ka'b said: a man among them would be with his wife on their bed, and both had become two stones. He said: 'Umar ibn 'Abd al-'Aziz asked me, and I mentioned that to him, so he called for a kharitah (a pouch, a bag of cloth or leather tied shut over its contents) that had been found in Egypt, and he took out from it fruit, dirhams and dinars, and indeed they were stones. As-Suddi said: this was one of the nine signs.

(And harden their hearts): Ibn 'Abbas said: that is, prevent them from faith. It has also been said: make them hard and seal them so that they do not open up to faith; the meaning is one. "So they will not believe" (fa-la yu'minu): it has been said that it is coordinated (ma'tuf) with His saying "liyudillu," meaning: We gave them blessings so that they would go astray and not believe, as al-Zajjaj and al-Mubarrad said. In that case there is nothing of the sense of supplication in it, and His saying "Our Lord, obliterate... and harden" is a parenthetical statement. Al-Farra', al-Kisa'i and Abu 'Ubaydah said: it is a supplication, so it is in the jussive position according to them, meaning: "O Allah, may they not believe" (fa-la yu'minu), that is, "may they not have believed." From this is the saying of al-A'sha:

So what has contracted between your eyes will not expand, and you will not meet me except with your nose humbled.

That is, "may it not expand." Whoever says "liyudillu" is a supplication, meaning "test them with straying," says that "fa-la yu'minu" is coordinated with it. It has also been said: it is in the accusative position because it is an answer to the imperative, meaning: "and harden their hearts, so they will not believe." This is also the view of al-Akhfash and al-Farra'. Al-Farra' recited:

O she-camel, proceed with a wide stride to Sulayman, that we may rest.

In that case the nun was dropped because it is in the accusative.

(until they see the painful punishment): Ibn 'Abbas said: it is drowning. Some people have found this verse problematic and said: how did he supplicate against them when the rule for the messengers is to seek the faith of their people? The answer is that it is not permissible for a prophet to supplicate against his people except with permission from Allah and notification that there is no one among them who will believe and that no one who will believe will emerge from their loins. The proof is His saying to Nuh, peace be upon him: ﴿Indeed, none of your people will believe except those who have already believed﴾ [11:36]. At that point he said: "My Lord, do not leave upon the earth from among the disbelievers any dwelling one" [71:26]. And Allah knows best.

Al-Qurtubi's commentary on Surah 10, verse 89:

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿He said: Your supplication has been answered﴾. Abu al-'Aliyah said: Musa supplicated and Harun said "Amin," so Harun is described as having said it [[من ع وك وهـ.]]. One who says "amin" to a supplication is himself a supplicant, since saying "amin" to supplication means saying "amin," and your saying "amin" is a supplication, meaning: O Lord, answer me. It was also said: Harun supplicated together with Musa. The scholars of meanings (ahl al-ma'ani) said: The Arabs sometimes address one person with the dual form of address. The poet said:

"I said to my companion, 'Do not hasten us
in uprooting its roots, so cut down the wormwood.'"

This is on the basis that "amin" is not a supplication and that Harun did not supplicate. Al-Nahhas said: I heard 'Ali ibn Sulayman say: The evidence that the supplication was made by both of them is the saying of Musa, peace be upon him, "Our Lord" (rabbana), and he did not say "My Lord" (rabbi). 'Ali and al-Sulami read "da'awatukuma" in the plural. Ibn al-Sumayqa read "ajabtu da'watakuma," as a report from God, Exalted is He, and put "da'wata" after it in the accusative. The discussion of "amin" has already been given in full at the end of al-Fatihah [[راجع ج ١ ص ١٢٧.]]. It is among the things that were specific to our Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ), Harun and Musa, peace be upon them. Anas ibn Malik narrated that the Messenger of God (ﷺ) said: "God has given my community three things that He has given to no one before them: the salam, which is the greeting of the people of Paradise; the rows of the angels; and amin, except for what was given to Musa and Harun." Al-Tirmidhi al-Hakim mentioned it in Nawadir al-Usul. It has already been mentioned in al-Fatihah [[راجع ج ١ ص ١٢٧.]].

His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So remain steadfast﴾. Al-Farra' and others said: This is a command to steadfastness, upon their command and persistence in it, in calling Pharaoh and his people to faith, until the fulfilment of the answer comes to them. Muhammad ibn 'Ali and Ibn Jurayj said: Pharaoh and his people remained for forty years after this answer, and then they were destroyed. It was also said: "So remain steadfast" means in the supplication, and steadfastness in supplication is leaving off hastiness in attaining the desired goal. Hastiness does not fall away from the heart except by the steadfastness of tranquillity in it, and that tranquillity is only attained through a good contentment with everything that appears from the unseen.

(And do not follow the way of those who do not know). It is read with a doubled nun in a place of jussive mood, as a prohibition, and the nun is for emphasis (tawkid). It was vowelled because of the meeting of two unvowelled letters, and kasra was chosen for it because it resembles the nun of the dual. Ibn Dhakwan read it with a single nun, as a negation. It was also said that it is a circumstantial clause (hal) from "istaqima," meaning: remain steadfast without following. The meaning is: do not take the path of those who do not know the reality of My promise and My threat.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 10, verse 90:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We brought the Children of Israel across the sea﴾. This was discussed earlier in al-Baqarah, in His saying: "And when We divided the sea for you" [[See vol. 1, p. 387.]]. Al-Hasan recited "wa-jawwaznā," and both are two dialects (lughatān).

(﴿Then Pharaoh and his hosts pursued them﴾). It is said: tabi'a and atba'a have one meaning, when one catches up with someone and overtakes him. Ittaba'a (with the shaddah) means when one travels behind him. Al-Asma'i said: atba'ahu (with the hamzah cut) means when one catches up with him and overtakes him, while ittaba'ahu (with the hamzah joined) means when one follows his trail, whether he overtakes him or not. Abu Zayd said the same. Qatadah recited "fa-ittaba'ahum" with the hamzah joined. It is also said: "ittaba'ahu" (with the hamzah joined) in a matter means he followed his example; and "atba'ahu" (with the hamzah cut) means [he followed him with] good or evil, this is the saying of Abu 'Amr. It has also been said that both have one meaning. Moses set out with the Children of Israel, and they were six hundred thousand and twenty thousand, and Pharaoh pursued them at morning with two thousand thousand and six hundred thousand. This has already been mentioned [[See vol. 1, p. 389.]].

(﴿Transgressively﴾) is in the accusative as a state (ḥāl).

(﴿And aggressively﴾) is coordinated with it, meaning in a state of transgression, aggression and injustice. It is said: ʿadā yaʿdū ʿadwan, like ghazā yaghzū ghazwan. Al-Hasan recited "wa-ʿadwan" with a damma on the ʿayn and the dal and a shaddah on the waw, like ʿalā yaʿlū ʿulūwan. The exegetes said: "baghyan" means seeking to exalt oneself without right in speech, and "ʿadwan" in action; so both are in the accusative as an object of purpose (maf'ūl lahu).

(﴿Until, when drowning overtook him﴾), meaning it reached him and attained him.

(﴿He said: "I believe"﴾), meaning I affirmed.

(﴿that﴾), meaning that.

(﴿there is no god except He in whom the Children of Israel believe﴾). When the preposition was omitted, the verb became transitive and took the accusative. It is also read with a kasrah, meaning "I became a believer," and then it resumes as a new sentence. Abu Hatim claimed that the verb "qāla" (he said) is elided, meaning "I believed, so I said that..." and faith does not benefit at that point, since repentance is accepted before seeing the punishment (ba's), but after it and after the matter has become manifest it is not accepted, as its explanation was mentioned earlier in al-Nisa' [[See vol. 5, p. 90.]]. It is said that Pharaoh feared entering the sea, and he was on a dark bay horse, and there was no female mare among Pharaoh's horses. Then Gabriel came on a mare in heat (wadīq, i.e., one desiring the stallion) [[i.e., one desiring the stallion.]], in the form of Haman, and said to him: "Go forward." Then he plunged into the sea and Pharaoh's horse followed her, while Michael drove them so that not one of them strayed. When the last of them was in the sea and the first of them wanted to come out, the sea closed over them, and drowning overpowered Pharaoh, so he said: "I believe in Him in whom the Children of Israel believe," and Gabriel pushed the mud of the sea into his mouth.

Al-Tirmidhi related from Ibn ʿAbbas that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "When God drowned Pharaoh, he said: 'I believe that there is no god except He in whom the Children of Israel believe.' Gabriel said: 'O Muhammad, if you had seen me as I took the mud of the sea and pushed it into his mouth, for fear that mercy would reach him.'" Abu ʿIsa said: this is a ḥasan hadith. Ḥāl al-baḥr: the black clay that is in its earth, as the lexicographers said. And from Ibn ʿAbbas, from the Prophet (ﷺ), he mentioned: "That Gabriel began to push mud into Pharaoh's mouth, for fear that he would say 'there is no god but God' and God would have mercy on him, or for fear that he would have mercy on him." He said: this is a ḥasan gharīb ṣaḥīḥ hadith. ʿAwn ibn ʿAbd Allah said: It reached me that Gabriel said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "No offspring of Iblis is more hateful to me than Pharaoh, for when drowning overtook him he said: 'I believe,' the verse, so I feared he would say it and be shown mercy, so I took a handful of earth or clay and stuffed it into his mouth." It is also said that he did this to him as a punishment for the enormity of what he used to do. Ka'b al-Ahbar said: God held back the Nile of Egypt from flowing in his time. The Copts said to him: "If you are our lord, then make the water flow for us." So he mounted and ordered his troops, commander by commander, and they began to stand at their ranks, and he leapt where they could not see him, dismounted from his animal, put on other garments, prostrated and humbled himself before God the Exalted, so God made the water flow for him. Then Gabriel came to him, alone, in the appearance of one seeking a fatwa, and said: "What does the Amir say about a man who has a slave who grew up in his bounty, with no master besides him, who then denied his favors, rejected his right, and claimed lordship over him?" So Pharaoh wrote: "Abu al-ʿAbbas al-Walid ibn Mus'ab ibn al-Rayyan says: his recompense is that he be drowned in the sea." Gabriel took it, and passed on, and when drowning overtook him, Gabriel, peace be upon him, handed him his decree.

This was already transmitted in al-Baqarah [[See vol. 1, pp. 381ff.]] from ʿAbd Allah ibn ʿAmr ibn al-ʿAs and Ibn ʿAbbas with chains, and this occurred on the day of ʿAshura, as its explanation was mentioned earlier in al-Baqarah too, so there is no point in repeating it.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And I am of the Muslims﴾, meaning of the monotheists who submit in obedience and compliance.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 10, verse 91:

It was said: it is from the speech of Allah, exalted is He. And it was said: it is from the speech of Jibril (Gabriel). And it was said: it is from the speech of Mika'il (Michael), or of other angels, may the blessings of Allah be upon them [[from ‘ayn and ha’ (manuscript sigla).]]. And it was said: it is from the words of Pharaoh within himself, and there was no speech of the tongue there; rather that occurred in his heart, so he said within himself what he said, when repentance did not benefit him. Its parallel is the verse ﴿Indeed, we feed you only for the sake of Allah's countenance﴾ [[See vol. 19, p. 125 onward.]] [al-Insan: 9]. The Lord praised them for what was in their inner selves, not that they uttered that with their tongues, and true speech is the speech of the heart.

**The Words of Allah Most High: ﴿So today We will save you in your body (bi-badanika)﴾**, meaning: We will cast you upon a *najwa* (a high place) of the earth.

The reason is that the Children of Israel did not believe that Pharaoh had drowned. They said, "He is greater in status than that." So Allah cast him upon a *najwa* of the earth, meaning a raised place by the sea, until they saw him.

Abu AwS ibn Hajar said, describing rain:

*"He who is in its 'aqwa is like he who is in its najwa,*
*and the one who hides is like one who walks in the open sun."*

[[The *'aqwa* and *'aqa'* are the courtyard, what surrounds the house, and the quarter; its plural is *'aqa'*. The *qarwah* is land exposed to the sun.]]

Al-Yazidi and Ibn al-Sumayqa recited *nunahhika* with the *ha'* (from *tanhiya*, "to move away"), and 'Alqamah related it from Ibn Mas'ud. The meaning is: you will be on one side of the sea. Ibn Jurayj said: he was thrown onto the sea shore until the Children of Israel saw him. He was short, red, and like a bull.

'Alqamah also related from 'Abd Allah (Ibn Mas'ud) that he recited *bi-nidaika* (with your call), from *nida'* (calling). Abu Bakr al-Anbari said: this does not contradict the orthography of our *mushaf* (Qur'anic codex), since it should be written with a *ya'* and a *kaf* after the *dal*, because the *alif* is dropped from *nidaika* in the arrangement of the codex's script, just as it is dropped from *al-zulumat* and *al-samawat*. When the deletion occurs, the spelling of *badanika* and *nidaika* becomes the same. However, this recitation is disfavored because it is anomalous (*shadhdh*) and differs from what the general body of Muslims holds. Recitation is a *sunna* (established practice) that a later generation takes from an earlier one. Its meaning falls short of the interpretation of our recitation, because it contains no mention of the *dir'* (coat of mail), which is the subject of the reports, consecutively transmitted, that the Children of Israel disputed about Pharaoh's drowning, and asked Allah Most High to show them him drowned. So they cast him upon a *najwa* of the earth in his body, and his body was wearing his *dir'*, which he wore in battles.

Ibn 'Abbas and Muhammad ibn Ka'b al-Qurazi said: his coat of mail was of strung pearls. It was also said: it was of gold, by which he was recognized. And it was said: it was of iron; this was said by Abu Sakhr. The *badan* is a short coat of mail.

Abu 'Ubayda recited, from al-A'sha:

*"And a white (coat of mail), like a pool, woven tightly,*
*for which there is a crest above the collar of the badan."*

[[*Al-bayda'* means the coat of mail. *Al-nahy* (with a fatha or kasra) means a pond, and every place where water gathers. *Al-mawdunah* means a woven coat of mail. *Al-qawnas* is the top of a helmet of iron.]]

He also recited, for 'Amr ibn Ma'd Yakrib:

*"Their women went with every wide coat of mail,*
*strongly woven and complete, and with the abdan."*

[[In 'a and h: *mashaa* (instead of *madaa*). *Al-mufadah* (with a damma on its first letter) means a wide coat of mail. *Al-jadla'* means a tightly woven coat of mail.]]

Ka'b ibn Malik said:

*"You see the abdan on them, fully covering,*
*on the heroes, and the sturdy yalab."*

He meant by *al-abdan* the coats of mail, and by *al-yalab*, the Yemeni coats of mail, which were made from hides stitched one to another. It is a collective noun; its singular is *yalabah*. 'Amr ibn Kulthum said:

*"Upon us are the white (swords) and the Yemeni yalab,*
*and swords that stand and bend."*

It was also said that *"bi-badanika"* means with a body without a soul. This was said by Mujahid. Al-Akhfash said: as for the statement of those who say *bi-dir'ika* (with your coat of mail), it is worthless. Abu Bakr said: because when they humbly asked Allah to let them witness Pharaoh drowned, He showed him to them, and they saw a body with no soul. When the Children of Israel saw it, they said, "Yes, O Musa! This is Pharaoh, and he has drowned," and doubt left their hearts. The sea had swallowed Pharaoh as it had been.

Accordingly, *"nunajjika bi-badanika"* carries two meanings. One: We will cast you upon a *najwa* of the earth. The second: We will display your body, which has no soul.

The anomalous recitation *"bi-nidaika"* returns in meaning to the recitation of the community, because *al-nida'* is interpreted in two ways. One: We will cast you by your crying out with the word of repentance, and by your saying, after its door was closed and the time for its acceptance had passed: ﴿I believe that there is no god except He in whom the Children of Israel believe, and I am of the Muslims﴾ [Yunus: 90], upon an elevated place. The other: ﴿So today We will remove you from the deep sea by your call﴾, when you said, "I am your Lord, the Most High." So his being saved in his body was a punishment from the Lord of the worlds for what had passed of his disbelief, which included his call in which he slandered and lied, and claimed power and a command about which he knew he was lying, incapable, and not deserving of it. Abu Bakr al-Anbari said: our recitation includes the meanings in the anomalous recitation and adds to them.

**The Words of Allah Most High: ﴿so that you may be a sign to those who come after you﴾**, meaning: to the Children of Israel and to those of Pharaoh's people who remained, who were not reached by the drowning and to whom this report had not come.

**(And indeed many among mankind are heedless of Our signs)**, meaning: they turn away from reflecting upon Our signs and contemplating them.

It was also read *"li-man khalafaka"* (with a fatha on the *lam*), meaning: for those who remain after you and succeed you in your land. 'Ali ibn Abi Talib recited *"li-man khalaqaka"* with a *qaf*, meaning: a sign for your Creator.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿If you are in doubt about what We have sent down to you﴾. The address is to the Prophet ﷺ, but the intended meaning is others. That is, you are not in doubt, but others were in doubt.

Abu Umar Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahid al-Zahid said: I heard the two imams Tha'lab and al-Mubarrad say: The meaning of "If you are in doubt" is: Say, O Muhammad, to the disbeliever, "If you are in doubt about what We have sent down to you, (then ask those who recite the Scripture before you)." That is, O worshipper of idols, if you are in doubt about the Qur'an, then ask those among the Jews who have embraced Islam, meaning Abdullah ibn Salam and those like him. This is because the idol-worshippers used to acknowledge that the Jews were more knowledgeable than them, because they were people of a Scripture. So the Messenger ﷺ called them to ask those whom they acknowledged to be more knowledgeable than them: Has God sent a messenger after Moses?

Al-Qutabi said: This is an address to one who could not definitively judge Muhammad ﷺ either as a liar or as truthful, but was in doubt.

It was also said: The address is to the Prophet ﷺ alone and not others, and the meaning is: If doubt were to reach you concerning what We have informed you of, then ask the People of the Book, and they would remove the doubt from you.

It was also said: Doubt here means constriction of the chest. That is, if your chest is constricted by the disbelief of these people, then be patient, and ask those who recite the Scripture before you, and they will inform you of the patience of the prophets before you in the face of the harm of their peoples, and how the outcome of their affair turned out.

In language, the root meaning of doubt (shakk) is constriction. It is said: shakka al-thawb, meaning he fastened it with a skewer until it became like a container. Likewise the travel bag (al-sufra) is pulled tight by its cords until it contracts. So doubt grips the chest and gathers it until it becomes constricted.

Al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl said: The fa' (fa) with conditional particles does not necessitate the verb nor affirm it. The evidence for this is what is narrated from the Prophet ﷺ, that when this verse was revealed he said: "By Allah, I will not doubt," then he resumed speech and said: ﴿Truth has come to you from your Lord, so do not be among the doubters﴾, that is, the sceptics, the hesitant.

﴿And do not be among those who denied the signs of Allah, lest you be among the losers﴾. The address in these two verses is to the Prophet ﷺ, and the intended meaning is others.

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿If you are in doubt about what We have sent down to you﴾. The address is to the Prophet ﷺ, but the intended meaning is others. That is, you are not in doubt, but others were in doubt.

Abu Umar Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahid al-Zahid said: I heard the two imams Tha'lab and al-Mubarrad say: The meaning of "If you are in doubt" is: Say, O Muhammad, to the disbeliever, "If you are in doubt about what We have sent down to you, (then ask those who recite the Scripture before you)." That is, O worshipper of idols, if you are in doubt about the Qur'an, then ask those among the Jews who have embraced Islam, meaning Abdullah ibn Salam and those like him. This is because the idol-worshippers used to acknowledge that the Jews were more knowledgeable than them, because they were people of a Scripture. So the Messenger ﷺ called them to ask those whom they acknowledged to be more knowledgeable than them: Has God sent a messenger after Moses?

Al-Qutabi said: This is an address to one who could not definitively judge Muhammad ﷺ either as a liar or as truthful, but was in doubt.

It was also said: The address is to the Prophet ﷺ alone and not others, and the meaning is: If doubt were to reach you concerning what We have informed you of, then ask the People of the Book, and they would remove the doubt from you.

It was also said: Doubt here means constriction of the chest. That is, if your chest is constricted by the disbelief of these people, then be patient, and ask those who recite the Scripture before you, and they will inform you of the patience of the prophets before you in the face of the harm of their peoples, and how the outcome of their affair turned out.

In language, the root meaning of doubt (shakk) is constriction. It is said: shakka al-thawb, meaning he fastened it with a skewer until it became like a container. Likewise the travel bag (al-sufra) is pulled tight by its cords until it contracts. So doubt grips the chest and gathers it until it becomes constricted.

Al-Husayn ibn al-Fadl said: The fa' (fa) with conditional particles does not necessitate the verb nor affirm it. The evidence for this is what is narrated from the Prophet ﷺ, that when this verse was revealed he said: "By Allah, I will not doubt," then he resumed speech and said: ﴿Truth has come to you from your Lord, so do not be among the doubters﴾, that is, the sceptics, the hesitant.

﴿And do not be among those who denied the signs of Allah, lest you be among the losers﴾. The address in these two verses is to the Prophet ﷺ, and the intended meaning is others.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 10, verse 96–97:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, those upon whom the word of your Lord has been justified will not believe﴾. This has already been discussed in this surah [[See p. 340 of this part.]]. Qatadah said: That is, those upon whom the anger and wrath of Allah have been decreed because of their disobedience, they will not believe.

(And even if every sign should come to them) He made "kull" feminine according to the meaning, that is, even if the signs ("al-ayat") should come to them.

(Until they see the painful punishment) Then, at that time, they will believe, but it will not benefit them.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 10, verse 98:

His saying, may He be exalted: (Why was there not a town that believed, so that its faith would benefit it?) Al-Akhfash and al-Kisa'i said: that is, "fa-hallā" (why not, would that). In the codex of Ubayy and Ibn Mas'ud it reads "fa-hallā." The original meaning of "lawlā" in speech is incitement (tahdid, urging), or an indication of the prevention of one thing due to the existence of another. What is understood from the meaning of the verse is the negation of faith among the people of the towns, then He made an exception for the people of Yunus. So, in terms of wording, it is an exception of the disconnected type (istithna' munqati'), but in terms of meaning it is connected (muttasil), because its implied sense is: no town's people believed except the people of Yunus.

The accusative case in "qawma" (the people of) is the preferred reading, and Sibawayh likewise placed it in the chapter of "that which is only ever in the accusative" (bab ma la yakunu illa mansuban). Al-Nahhas said: "illa qawma Yunus" is in the accusative because it is an exception not from the first part, meaning "but the people of Yunus"; this is the view of al-Kisa'i, al-Akhfash and al-Farra'. It is also permissible to read "illa qawma Yunus" in the nominative (raf'). Among the best that has been said regarding the nominative is what Abu Ishaq al-Zajjaj said: the meaning would be "other than the people of Yunus," and when "illa" came, the noun after it took the case of "ghayr" (other than), as the poet said:

"And every brother who is parted from his brother ... by the life of your father, except the two Farqadan."

It is related in the account of the people of Yunus, from a group of the exegetes, that the people of Yunus were in Nineveh, in the land of Mosul, and they worshipped idols. Allah sent Yunus, peace be upon him, to call them to Islam and to abandon what they were upon, but they refused. It is said that he kept calling them for nine years, and then he despaired of their faith. It was said to him: "Inform them that the punishment will come upon them in the morning after three (days)," and he did so. They said: "He is a man who does not lie. Watch him: if he remains with you and among you, then there is no harm upon you; but if he departs from you, then it is the descent of punishment without doubt." When night came, Yunus took provisions and went out from them. In the morning they found him gone, so they repented, called upon Allah, wore sackcloth, separated the mothers from the children among the people and the animals, and restored the wrongful gains in that state. Ibn Mas'ud said: "A man would come to a stone on which he had laid the foundation of his building, pull it up, and return it." The punishment that came upon them, as related from Ibn 'Abbas, was (hovering) over a distance of two-thirds of a mile. It is also related as one mile. From Ibn 'Abbas also: a cloud covered them, and in it was redness, and it kept drawing closer until they felt its heat between their shoulders. Ibn Jubayr said: the punishment enveloped them as a cloth covers a grave. Then, when their repentance was sound, Allah lifted the punishment from them.

Al-Tabari said: the people of Yunus were singled out from among all the nations in that they were forgiven after witnessing the punishment, and this was mentioned from a group of the exegetes. Al-Zajjaj said: the punishment did not actually befall them; they only saw the sign that indicates the punishment. Had they seen the very punishment, faith would not have benefited them.

I say: the saying of al-Zajjaj is good, for the witnessing with which repentance does not benefit is being actually seized by the punishment, as in the story of Pharaoh. For this reason the story of the people of Yunus was brought right after the story of Pharaoh, because he believed when he saw the punishment and that did not benefit him, whereas the people of Yunus repented before that. This is supported by his saying, peace be upon him: "Allah accepts the repentance of the servant as long as he has not begun the death-rattle (yughargir)." The "gharghara" is the rattling in the throat, and that is the state of being seized by death; before that it is not so. And Allah knows best.

It has also been related, with the same meaning as what we have said, from Ibn Mas'ud, that when Yunus promised them the punishment within three days, he went out from them; in the morning they found him gone, so they repented and separated the mothers from the children. This indicates that their repentance came before seeing the sign of the punishment. It will come with a connected chain (musnad) and explained in surah "al-Saffat" [[see vol. 15, p. 121]], God willing, may He be exalted.

The meaning of (We removed from them the punishment of disgrace in the life of this world) is: the punishment which Yunus had promised them would descend upon them, not that they actually saw it face to face nor that it appeared to them. On this reading there is no difficulty, no contradiction and no restriction. And Allah knows best.

In sum, the people of Nineveh were, in the prior knowledge of Allah, among the blessed. It was related from Ali, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: "Caution does not turn back decree, but supplication indeed turns back decree." That is because Allah, may He be exalted, says: "Except the people of Yunus; when they believed, We removed from them the punishment of disgrace in the life of this world." He, may Allah be pleased with him, said: "That was the day of 'Ashura'."

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We let them enjoy for a time﴾. It was said: "until their appointed term," said al-Suddi. It was also said: "until they arrive at Paradise or the Fire," said Ibn 'Abbas.

"His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if your Lord had willed, those on earth would have believed, all of them, together﴾ — meaning: He would have compelled them to it."

"Kulluhum" (all of them) is an emphatic (ta'kid) for "man" (those). "Jami'an" (together) — according to Sibawayh, it is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (hal). Al-Akhfash said: it came after "kull" as an emphasis, like His saying: ﴿Do not take two gods﴾ [[See vol. 10, p. 113.]] [al-Nahl: 51].

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Would you then compel the people until they become believers?﴾ Ibn 'Abbas said: The Prophet (ﷺ) was eager for the faith of all people, so Allah, exalted is He, informed him that none believes except those for whom happiness had preceded in the First Reminder (al-dhikr al-awwal), and none goes astray except those for whom wretchedness had preceded in the First Reminder. It has also been said: what is meant by "the people" here is Abu Talib, and this too is from Ibn 'Abbas.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And it is not for any soul to believe except by the permission of Allah﴾. "Mā" is a negation, meaning: it is not fitting for any soul to believe except by His decree, His destiny, His will, and His volition.

﴿And He places the abomination﴾. Al-Hasan, Abu Bakr and al-Mufaddal read "wa-najʿalu" with the nūn, as a plural of majesty (ʿalā al-taʿẓīm). Ar-rijs (الرِّجْسُ) means the punishment. Its rāʾ may be pronounced with ḍamma or kasra; both are two dialectal forms (lughatān).

﴿upon those who do not reason﴾, meaning they do not reason about the command of Allah, exalted and majestic is He, and His prohibition.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 10, verse 101:

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿Say: Look at what is in the heavens and the earth﴾ are a command to the disbelievers to take heed and to reflect upon the created things which point to the Creator, the One Who is capable of perfection. The discussion of this meaning has already been given in more than one place, in full [[See vol. 7, p. 330.]].

﴿And signs and warnings avail not﴾: "ma" here is a negation, meaning "and will not avail." It has also been said that it is interrogative, the sense being: "what avails?" (ma tughni, "what avails"?)

﴿The signs﴾: that is, the proofs (al-dalalat).

﴿And the warnings﴾: that is, the messengers (al-rusul), plural of nadhir (warner), and it is the Messenger (ﷺ).

﴿For a people who do not believe﴾: that is, for those for whom it has already been decreed in the knowledge of Allah that they will not believe.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 10, verse 102:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Do they then await anything but the like of the days of those who passed away before them?﴾ Al-ayyam (the days) here means the events (al-waqa'i'), as one says: "So-and-so is knowledgeable in the ayyam of the Arabs," meaning in their events. Qatadah said: it means the events of Allah concerning the people of Nuh, 'Ad, Thamud and others. The Arabs call punishment "days" and blessings "days," as in His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And remind them of the Days of Allah﴾ [see vol. 9, p. 341]. Everything that has passed for you of good or evil is "days."

(So await) i.e., wait in expectation (tarabbusu). This is a threat and a warning.

(Indeed, I am with you among those who await.) I.e., those who wait for the appointed time of my Lord.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 10, verse 103:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Then We save Our messengers and those who believe﴾, meaning: according to Our custom, when We send down a punishment upon a people, We bring out the messengers and the believers from among them. The "thumma" (then) here means: then know that We save Our messengers.

(Thus it is incumbent upon Us) meaning: obligatory upon Us, because He has informed of it, and there is no contradiction in His report. Ya'qub read "thumma nunajjee" with a light (mukhaffafah) pronunciation. Al-Kisa'i, Hafs and Ya'qub read "nunji al-mu'minin" with a light pronunciation, while the rest read it with a doubled (shaddah) pronunciation. Both are eloquent dialects: anja yunji injaan (andja) and najja yunajji tanjiyah (najja), with the same meaning.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿Say, "O mankind..."﴾ He means the disbelievers of Makkah.

(If you are in doubt about my religion) that is, if you are in doubt about the religion of Islam to which I call you.

(Then I do not worship those whom you worship besides Allah) from the idols, which do not understand.

(But I worship Allah, who causes you to die) that is, who makes you die and takes your souls.

(And I have been commanded to be among the believers) i.e., those who affirm the signs of their Lord.

**Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on Surah 10, verses 105–106:**

His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And that you set your face﴾. "That" (an) is coordinated with "that I should be" (an akuna), meaning: it was said to me, "Be among the believers, and set your face," i.e., direct your face (to the religion). Ibn ʿAbbas said: "Your deed." It was also said: "Your self," meaning: be upright by turning your attention to what you were commanded regarding the religion.

(Hanifan) means upright in it, inclining away from every other religion. Hamzah ibn ʿAbd al-Muttalib, may Allah be pleased with him, said:[[From manuscript ʿ.]]

*You praised Allah when He guided my heart*
*away from associating partners, to the upright (hanif) religion.*

Its derivation has already been discussed in *al-Anʿam*,[[See vol. 8, p. 28. The author discussed it fully in al-Baqarah; see vol. 2, p. 129.]] and praise is due to Allah.

(And do not be among the polytheists.) That is, it was said to me: "And do not associate," and the address is to him while the intended meaning is others. Likewise His saying: (And do not call upon) means: do not worship, (other than Allah what neither benefits you) if you worship it, (nor harms you) if you disobey Him.

(But if you do) meaning: if you worship other than Allah, (then indeed you would be, at that time, among the wrongdoers), meaning those who place worship in other than its proper place.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 10, verse 107:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And if Allah touches you with harm﴾, i.e., afflicts you with it.

(﴿There is no remover of it except Him﴾), i.e., there is no repeller of it except Him. (﴿And if He intends for you good﴾), i.e., He afflicts you with ease and blessing.

(﴿There is no repeller of His bounty, which He causes to reach whomever He wills of His servants﴾), i.e., with whatever He wills of good and evil. (﴿And He is the Forgiving, the Merciful﴾) — Forgiving of the sins and transgressions of His servants, and Merciful toward His friends (awliya') in the Hereafter.

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 10, verse 108:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Say: O mankind, the truth has come to you from your Lord﴾, meaning the Qur'an. It was also said: the Messenger (ﷺ).

(﴿Whoever is guided⁠﴾) meaning: whoever confirms Muhammad and believes in what he brought.

(﴿then he is only guided for [the benefit of] himself⁠﴾) meaning: for the deliverance of his own soul.

(﴿And whoever goes astray⁠﴾) meaning: whoever abandons the Messenger and the Qur'an and follows the idols and images.

(﴿then he only goes astray to its detriment⁠﴾) meaning: the burden of that falls upon himself.

(﴿And I am not over you a manager⁠﴾) meaning: not a guardian who keeps watch over your deeds; I am only a messenger. Ibn 'Abbas said: it was abrogated by the verse of the sword (ayat al-sayf) (i.e., a verse that cancels an earlier ruling, naskh).

Commentary of al-Qurtubi (al-Jami' li-Ahkam al-Quran) on surah 10, verse 109:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And follow what is revealed to you, and be patient﴾. It was said: it has been abrogated (mansukh) by the verse of fighting (ayat al-qital). And it was said: it is not abrogated, and its meaning is: be patient in obedience and patient in refraining from disobedience. Ibn 'Abbas said: When it was revealed, the Prophet ﷺ gathered the Ansar and gathered no one else with them, and said: "Indeed you will find, after me, favoritism (athara) [[i.e., he will favor others over you in their share of the fay' (spoils).]], so be patient until you meet me at the Pool (al-Hawd)." And it is narrated from Anas in similar terms. Then Anas said: They did not endure patiently, so he commanded them to be patient just as Allah the Exalted had commanded him. And in this regard 'Abd al-Rahman ibn Hassan says:

Unquestionably, convey to Mu'awiya ibn Harb, Commander of the Believers, my speech (nathaa) [[Nathaa in speech is applied to both the ugly and the good.]]

That we are patient, and that we will wait for you until the Day of Mutual Loss and Dispute.

﴿Until Allah judges, and He is the best of judges﴾ — an inchoative and a predicate (ibtida' wa khabar), because He, Mighty and Majestic, judges only with truth.

The surah of Yunus is complete, and praise belongs to Allah alone.
